segments.text: Far, far away, at the very top of the world, there is a place where it is winter almost all year long. It is called the North Pole.

At the North Pole, the snow is so deep that it comes up past your knees. It sparkles as if someone sprinkled sugar over everything: over the rooftops, over the fence posts, over the tall dark pine trees that stand in rows like sleepy giants. When you walk on it, it squeaks and crunches under your boots. Squeak. Crunch. Squeak. Crunch. The air is so cold that it tickles your nose and turns your breath into little white clouds.
And at night, the sky at the North Pole does something wonderful. It dances.

Long, shimmering ribbons of light swirl across the darkness: green as a Christmas tree, purple as a plum, and sometimes pink as a strawberry. They swish and sway and ripple, like curtains blowing in a gentle wind. These dancing lights have a name. They are called the northern lights, and they are one of the most magical things in the whole world. (They are real, too. If you ever travel far enough north on a clear winter night, you might see them yourself.)
Under the northern lights sits a little village, and oh, what a busy, cheerful place it is.

Narrow lanes of packed snow wind between the houses, lit by old-fashioned lampposts with round glass globes that glow like little orange moons. Along the lanes, the elves' cottages huddle close together to keep each other warm. They are painted every color you can imagine: raspberry red, butter yellow, peppermint green and robin's-egg blue. Their roofs are piled high with snow like thick white frosting, their round windows glow gold, and every front door wears its own tiny wreath. Every chimney puffs out a curl of smoke, so the whole village smells of wood fires and something baking.

And who lives in those cottages? The elves! North Pole elves are about as tall as a kitchen table, with pointed ears, rosy cheeks and quick, clever fingers. But no two elves look alike. Long ago, elves came to the North Pole from every corner of the world, so their skin is every shade you can imagine, and their hair is straight or wavy, curly or coily, black or brown or red or golden or silver. Some are young and bouncy, and some are very, very old. And all of them call the North Pole home. They wear knitted caps in every color of the rainbow, each one with a tiny bell on the tip, so wherever elves go, you hear them coming: jingle, jingle, jingle. They hum while they work, they sing while they walk, and they laugh at almost everything.
If you strolled down the main lane of the village, you would pass all sorts of wonderful little shops.

First comes the bakery, the Gingerbread Oven, run by Hazel Crumb, the head baker. Hazel is round and rosy as a fresh-baked bun, with warm brown skin and curly gray hair tucked under a tall white baker's hat, a red-and-white striped apron covered in floury handprints, and sleeves always rolled up to her elbows. She hums while she kneads the dough, and she always has a dusting of flour on the tip of her nose, which she never seems to notice. Its windows are fogged with warm steam, and the air smells of cinnamon, brown sugar and fresh bread. Next door is the candy shop, where elves pull long, stretchy ropes of peppermint and twist them into red-and-white stripes. Then the ribbon shop, run by Fern, a quick, quiet elf with two long black braids tied with green ribbon, and a rainbow of ribbons tied around her wrists, so she can always grab the right one in a hurry. Its shelves are stacked with spools of ribbon in every color, gold and silver, plaid and polka-dot, and the crinkle-crinkle of wrapping paper drifting out the door.

There is the North Pole Post Office, where letters from children all over the world arrive in big canvas sacks. The elves open every single one, read it carefully, and tuck it into a tall wall of wooden cubbies. The head of the post office is Juniper, who zooms between the cubbies in her wheelchair, its spokes painted like snowflakes, sorting letters faster than anyone else in the village. Whoosh, whoosh go the envelopes. There is the toy repair shop, where old, much-loved toys come to be mended: a teddy bear with a loose button eye, a wooden train with a wobbly wheel. The elf who mends them is Bob Mookie. He's tall for an elf and skinny as a candy cane, with a bushy white mustache that curls up at both ends, round spectacles perched on the tip of his nose, and a brown leather apron with pockets full of tiny screwdrivers and spools of thread. He has the biggest laugh in the whole village, a booming HA-HA-HOO that makes the toys on his shelves rattle. Once, just once, he went on vacation to a tropical island, and he has never stopped talking about it. If you ever smell pink guava cookies baking at the Gingerbread Oven, you can be sure Bob Mookie is somewhere nearby. And at the end of the lane stands a glass greenhouse that glows soft green in the dark. Inside it is warm and misty, full of plants from faraway places, and it belongs to someone you will meet very soon.

In the middle of the village is the square, with a giant spruce tree hung with lanterns and a frozen pond where elves skate in swirly circles after work. The fastest skater of all is Tiny Tamsin, the smallest elf in the village, no taller than a candlestick, with a cloud of dark curls and a puffy yellow coat, who giggles every single time she spins.

And biggest of all is Santa's workshop, a long wooden building with frosty windows and a crooked chimney, where elves build toys all year long. Even late at night you can hear them working: tap-tap-tap go their tiny hammers, whirr go their spinning wheels, and every so often a whole room of elves bursts into a happy song.
Next to the workshop is a big, cozy house with a red front door, and at the very top of the house is a tall arched window that always glows with golden light.
And in that house lives the most famous person at the North Pole.
Santa Claus.

Santa is tall and round, with a belly that jiggles when he laughs. His beard is long and white and fluffy, as white as fresh snow, and it reaches all the way down to the middle of his chest. His cheeks are rosy red, like two shiny winter apples, and his blue eyes twinkle like stars, as if he always knows a happy secret.

Santa wears a warm red coat trimmed with soft white fur, red trousers, and a wide black belt with a big gold buckle that shines in the lantern light. His tall black boots are polished so well that you could almost see your face in them. When he laughs, his laugh is deep and round and rumbly.
Ho, ho, ho!
It's a laugh that makes everyone nearby want to laugh too.
But on this night, Santa was not laughing.
Beside him walked his wife, Mrs. Claus.

Mrs. Claus is a little shorter than Santa, with kind, crinkly eyes behind small round spectacles. Her hair is silver mixed with gold, and she wears it in one long braid down her back, tied at the end with a green velvet ribbon. Over her red-and-green dress she wears a cranberry-colored cloak that swishes when she walks, and an apron with lots and lots of pockets.

And those pockets are full of surprises: seed packets, colored pencils, a magnifying glass, and a little sketchbook filled with drawings of flowers. That's because Mrs. Claus is a botanist. A botanist is a scientist who studies plants: flowers, trees, mosses and all things green and growing. Mrs. Claus knows more about plants than almost anyone in the world. And she has a special rule: when she finds a beautiful flower in the wild, she doesn't pick it. She draws it instead, so the flower can keep on growing.

On the very last page of that sketchbook was a drawing Mrs. Claus had never finished. It showed a small flower she had only ever read about in very old books: a wild orchid that blooms at the very edge of the snow. She had drawn its outline in pencil, but she had never colored it in.
Someday,
she liked to say,
I'll see it for myself. Then I'll know what colors it really is.
Pinned to her cloak, right over her heart, Mrs. Claus always wears a tiny silver brooch shaped like her very favorite flower: the twinflower.

The twinflower is a little plant that grows in the cool, shady forests of the far north. It creeps along the forest floor on thin green runners, with tiny round leaves that stay green even under the snow. In summer, it sends up a slender stem as thin as a thread. At the top, the stem splits in two, and from each side hangs one small pink bell, nodding down toward the moss. Always two, side by side, like a pair of best friends holding hands. That's why it's called the twinflower. And on a warm summer evening, the twinflower smells sweet, a little like vanilla.
Mrs. Claus loves the twinflower because it shares her name.

A long time ago, in a country called Sweden, there lived a scientist named Carl Linnaeus, who loved plants more than anything. He came up with a way of giving every plant and animal its very own name, and scientists all over the world still use it today.
The twinflower was Linnaeus's favorite flower, and it was named after him: Linnaea borealis, which means Linnaeus's flower of the north.
And when Mrs. Claus was a baby, her parents, who loved plants too, named her after that very same flower and the man who loved it. They named her Linnea (you say it lih-NAY-uh).
Most people call her Mrs. Claus. But Santa calls her by her first name, Linnea. And she calls Santa by his first name, which is Kris.

It was the very end of winter. At the North Pole, winter is a long, long night: from autumn until spring, the sun never rises at all, and the only light in the sky comes from the moon, the stars and the dancing northern lights. Now that long night was almost over. In just a few weeks, the sun would peek over the edge of the world for the first time in six months. Last Christmas was over, and next Christmas was far, far away.

That evening, just after supper, Santa and Mrs. Claus pulled on their warm coats to go and watch the reindeer practice. At the end of every winter, as the long night begins to fade, Santa's flying team practices every evening, so that they will be strong and ready by Christmas, even though Christmas is still far, far away. Santa loves to watch them fly. And Mrs. Claus never goes to the barn without bringing a treat.

So now they walked side by side through the snow. Crunch, crunch, crunch went Santa's big black boots. Crunch, crunch, crunch went Mrs. Claus's little red boots. Their lanterns swung back and forth, making golden circles on the snow, and Santa hummed a jolly little tune.
Over her arm, Mrs. Claus carried a wicker basket with a red checkered cloth tucked over the top. Whatever was inside smelled warm and buttery.

The path to the barn led right past Mrs. Claus's greenhouse. It glowed in the dark like a big glass lantern, soft green and gold, and its windows were fogged with warm mist. Mrs. Claus always peeked in as she passed, the way you might peek in on a sleeping baby, and tonight was no different.
If you could have pressed your nose to the glass beside her, here is what you would have seen.

One half of the greenhouse is Mrs. Claus's kitchen garden. Tomatoes hang red and round as Christmas ornaments. Strawberries peek out from under their leaves. There are rows of crunchy lettuce, fat orange carrots, and herbs that smell wonderful when you brush past them: mint, basil and dill. In one corner hums a wooden beehive, where the bees make golden honey from the greenhouse flowers. Almost everything the elves eat in winter grows right here.
The other half is her orchid room, and it is the most surprising place at the whole North Pole.

Here is why. Orchids are one of the biggest families of flowers in the world, and they grow almost everywhere: in steamy jungles and on windy mountaintops, in deserts and in swamps, on every continent except icy Antarctica. Some brave little orchids even grow far, far north on the Arctic tundra. But the North Pole itself isn't land at all. It is frozen ocean, a giant floating sheet of sea ice with no soil anywhere. Nothing grows there by itself. No trees, no grass, and not a single orchid.
Except in Mrs. Claus's greenhouse.

Where did all those orchids come from? Some were Christmas presents from Santa, who always seems to know exactly which orchid she has been hoping for. Some came from orchid growers, people who raise orchids in their own greenhouses, so that nobody ever needs to take one from the wild. Some she traded with friends from her orchid club, the Alaska Orchid Society, far to the south, where the members grow orchids under lights through the long, dark Alaskan winters, just like she does. They are always delighted when Mrs. Claus arrives by sleigh with a tin of cookies and a new plant to share. And a few, her very proudest, she grew herself from seed, which took years and years of patience.

How can you tell if a flower is an orchid? Mrs. Claus taught Santa the trick long ago. An orchid flower has three sepals (SEE-pulz), the outer parts that wrapped the bud before it opened, and three petals. But one of the petals is different from all the others. It is called the lip, and it is often the brightest, fanciest part of the flower, because it is the landing pad where insects touch down.

And right in the middle is the orchid's most special secret: the column. In most flowers, the part that makes pollen and the part that catches pollen grow separately. In an orchid, they are fused together into one little column. And in most orchids, the pollen isn't loose and dusty, the way it is in other flowers. It is packed into tiny sticky bundles called pollinia (pol-IN-ee-uh), which stick onto a visiting insect and ride away with it to the next flower.
Three sepals, three petals, one of them a lip, and a fused column in the middle,
Santa likes to say, counting on his fingers.
That's how you know it's an orchid.

And how does a greenhouse stay warm at the top of a frozen world? Deep, deep under the sea ice, on the bottom of the Arctic Ocean, there are hot springs where warmth from inside the Earth bubbles up. The elves built a long pipe that carries a little of that warmth up to the greenhouse, so the Earth itself keeps the orchids cozy. In summer, when the sun shines all day and all night at the North Pole, big barrels of water soak up the sunshine and hold on to its warmth for the long winter.

But in winter, the North Pole is dark for months and months, and plants need light. So along the greenhouse rafters hang Mrs. Claus's aurora lanterns: glass globes that each hold a wisp of captured northern light, glowing green and violet and pink. In our world, nobody knows how to catch the aurora's light. But at the North Pole, Mrs. Claus does. That part is magic.
Tonight, though, Mrs. Claus only looked through the glass for a moment.
Goodnight, my darlings,
she whispered to her orchids. Then she hurried on beside Santa.
They were going to the reindeer barn.

The reindeer barn is a big red building with a snowy roof and long, glittering icicles hanging from the edges like a crystal fringe. A wreath of pine and red berries hangs on its wide wooden doors, and above the doors hangs a row of silver sleigh bells. When the wind blows, the bells ring. Ting-a-ling-a-ling.
And above the barn, the sky was full of reindeer.

The northern lights were dancing, and Santa's flying team was out practicing, swooping and looping over the snowy roof, their harness bells ringing. Jingle, jingle, jingle! A crowd of elves stood in the snow below, cheering and pointing and waving their caps, so that their cap bells jingled too.

You probably know the names of Santa's flying team already, and here they were. Dasher, always first and always fastest, zooming ahead like a shooting star. Dancer, twirling loop-the-loops. Prancer, lifting her hooves high and proud, even in the air. Vixen, clever and curious, peeking down at everything below. Comet, quick and sparkly, leaving a trail of glittering frost. Cupid, gentle and kind, who always waits for whoever is last. And Donner, big and strong, whose snort rumbles like faraway thunder.
Santa stopped walking. He counted them, his lips moving. One, two, three, four, five, six, seven.
Seven,
he said slowly.
My team has eight. Where's Blitzen?

Just then, a small figure came running toward them through the snow, waving both arms. It was Marigold, the elf who looks after the reindeer, her cheeks pink from running through the cold. Marigold is sturdy and strong, with freckles across her nose and short copper-red hair sticking out from under a woolly brown hat, a padded green work coat with bits of hay stuck all over it, and big boots for tramping through deep snow. She always smells a little of hay and reindeer, and she talks to the reindeer as if they were her best friends, because they are.
Santa! Mrs. Claus!
she puffed.
Nobody is hurt. But you need to come and see Blitzen. Something's wrong. She can't fly.
Santa and Mrs. Claus looked at each other. Then they hurried to the barn as fast as their boots would carry them.
Santa pulled open the heavy doors. Creeeeak.

Warm air rushed out to meet them. Inside, the barn smelled wonderful, of sweet golden hay, fresh pine branches, and warm, woolly reindeer. Lanterns hung along the wooden beams, glowing like little suns. The floor was covered in soft straw that crackled underfoot. And through the cracks in the roof, the northern lights peeked in, painting stripes of green and purple across the walls.
Each reindeer had her own stall, with her name carved above it in curly letters.

Not all of Santa's reindeer pull the sleigh on Christmas Eve. The barn is home to a whole herd, a big reindeer family. There was Evenstar, the oldest and wisest of them all, with a silvery face and gentle eyes. Long ago, she pulled Santa's sleigh herself, and now she watches over the whole family. There was Whistler, who made a little whistling sound when she was excited. There was Bramble, sturdy and brave, with a coat as brown as chocolate. There was Starbloom, sweet and gentle, with a white spot on her forehead shaped like a star. And there was Lilt, the youngest of all, small and springy, with ears a bit too big for her head. Lilt was much too young to fly, but she dreamed about it every single night.

As the reindeer shifted and stepped in their stalls, you could hear a funny little sound. Click. Click. Click-click. The sound came from inside their feet! It's one of the ways reindeer keep track of each other, even in a snowstorm or in the dark. Click, click, click. Here I am. Click, click, click. Here we are.
Every one of Santa's reindeer is a girl, and every one of them wears a crown of antlers.

The reindeer of the North Pole have a secret. When the northern lights dance in the sky, the reindeer can feel it. A tingle starts in their hooves, tickle-tickle-tickle, like snowflakes landing on their toes. Then it rises up through their legs and along their backs, all the way to the tips of their antlers. That tingle means one thing: It's time to fly! And when it comes, their hooves begin to click faster and faster, click-click-click-click, like a drumroll, until every hoof on the team is clicking together in the very same rhythm. And then, up they go.
That night, the northern lights were dancing brighter than ever.

Inside the barn, the herd could feel it too. Evenstar lifted her silvery nose to the sky. Whistler went wheee! Starbloom's hooves went click-click-click. And little Lilt bounced up and down, boing, boing, boing, until her big ears flopped.
But in the very last stall, one reindeer stood very, very still.
Her name was Blitzen.

Blitzen was the strongest flier in the whole herd. Her coat was the warm brown color of cinnamon toast, with a creamy white patch on her chest. Her antlers curved up high like two brave branches. On a normal night, Blitzen could zoom through a snowstorm faster than a shooting star, and she loved it more than anything.
When the lantern light caught Blitzen's eyes, they glowed a deep, shimmering blue, like two little pieces of winter sky.
But tonight, Blitzen's hooves did not tingle. And they did not click. Not a single click.
She stretched her neck up toward the dancing sky. She took a deep breath that puffed out in a long white cloud, hhhhhhh. She waited for the tickle in her toes.
Nothing.
She tried a little hop. Thump. Her hooves landed right back in the straw.
She tried a bigger hop. Thump.
She gathered all her strength, every last bit, and jumped the biggest jump she had ever jumped.
THUMP.

Blitzen stood still. Her ears drooped down, down, down. Her tail stopped swishing. Her deep blue eyes filled with worry. Her tummy felt tight and heavy, the way your tummy feels when something you love to do suddenly feels hard.
Oh, Blitzen,
Santa said softly.
He knelt down in the straw beside her and laid his big warm hand on her side. Underneath his fingers, her heart went thump-thump, thump-thump, strong and steady. Santa stroked her soft fur.
Your heart is strong,
he said.
Your legs are strong. So why can't you fly, my dear?
Mrs. Claus knelt down on Blitzen's other side. She took out her magnifying glass and looked at Blitzen very carefully, the same careful way she looked at her plants.
She checked Blitzen's hooves. Clean and hard and strong.
She touched Blitzen's nose. Cool and damp, just right.
She peeked inside Blitzen's ears. Soft and pink and healthy.
She isn't hurt, Kris,
said Mrs. Claus gently.
She isn't sick. She isn't tired.
She tapped her magnifying glass against her chin, thinking.
It's as if the sky is singing her a song, and she just can't hear it right now.

Outside, the jingling had stopped. The flying team had landed, and one by one they crowded into the barn doorway: Dasher and Dancer, Prancer and Vixen, Comet and Cupid and Donner, their antlers still frosty from the sky. Inside, the herd had stopped prancing. The barn was so quiet now that you could hear the lanterns hiss softly and the wind sigh against the walls.

Whistler gave a small worried whistle. Whee-oo. Bramble stamped her hoof. Starbloom stretched over the wall of her stall and pressed her nose gently against Blitzen's cheek. And little Lilt tiptoed across the straw and leaned against her friend, warm and fuzzy, as if to say, I'm right here.

Santa's reindeer are like a choir, and each one sings her own special note. When they fly together, all their notes join into one beautiful song across the sky. Tonight, Blitzen's note had gone quiet. And when one reindeer cannot fly, the whole herd feels it, because they belong to each other.
Up above, the northern lights flickered through the cracks in the roof, green, then purple, then green again, as if the sky itself were calling softly, Blitzen? We're still here.
Blitzen lowered her head, and Santa wrapped both his arms around her neck.
Don't you worry,
he told her.
You are not in trouble, and you are not alone. We will figure this out together.

Mrs. Claus folded back the checkered cloth on her basket, and a warm smell of cinnamon and butter floated out. Inside were oatmeal cookies, still soft from the oven, and a tall thermos of hot cocoa. She poured two steaming mugs. The cocoa was sweet and chocolatey, with a cool tingle of peppermint at the end, and it warmed Santa all the way down to his toes.

Then Mrs. Claus reached into her apron pocket and held out a handful of something pale and crinkly, gray-green and soft, like a tiny sponge. It was lichen, the reindeer's very favorite winter food. Blitzen sniffed it. Then she nibbled it, crunch, crunch, and her ears lifted, just a little.
Then Santa stood up slowly and stroked his long white beard. That's what he always did when he was thinking very hard.
This isn't a problem we can fix with medicine,
he said.
Or a bandage, or a warm blanket, or an extra bucket of oats. This is something old. Very, very old.
Older than us?
asked Mrs. Claus.
Much older than us,
said Santa.
So we need to ask something that remembers more than we do.

Mrs. Claus's eyes began to sparkle behind her spectacles, the way they did whenever she spotted a rare flower peeking out of the snow. A smile spread slowly across her face, and the little silver twinflower on her cloak caught the light of the aurora and shone, just for a moment, pink and green.
The Library of Lost Winters,
she whispered.
Santa smiled back, and for the first time all night, his eyes began to twinkle again.
The Library of Lost Winters,
he said.

Blitzen lifted her head, just a little. Little Lilt's big ears popped straight up. And outside, the northern lights rippled across the sky like the pages of a giant book, turning and turning, as if the sky could hardly wait to see what would happen next.

Santa and Mrs. Claus left the warm barn and stepped back out into the cold night. The air was so crisp that it pinched their cheeks pink, and the snow creaked under their boots. Creak, creak, creak. Above them, the northern lights rippled green and violet, and the stars sparkled like spilled sugar.

They hurried up the lane to the big house with the red front door. Its windows glowed honey-gold, and smoke curled from both its chimneys. And at the very top of the house, the tall arched window shone brightest of all, like a big, kind eye that never goes to sleep.
Behind that window is the Library of Lost Winters.

To get there, you go through the red front door, past the crackling fireplace in the front hall, and up a twisty staircase that winds round and round and round, until you're a little dizzy and a little out of breath. And then, at the very top, you push open a round wooden door carved with snowflakes. Creeeak.
And there it is.

The Library of Lost Winters is the oldest room at the North Pole. It is tall and round, like the inside of a tower, and its walls are covered from floor to ceiling with books. Big books and tiny books. Fat books and skinny books. Books bound in red leather and green velvet and soft gray birch bark. Some are so old that their pages have turned the color of toast. The shelves go up so high that the top ones disappear into shadow, and to reach them there are tall wooden ladders that roll along brass rails. Rrrrrumble go their little wheels.

Lanterns glow amber between the shelves. Thin copper pipes run along the walls, carrying melted snow, and the water inside them chimes softly as it flows, tink, tink, tinkle, like faraway bells. The books lean together on the shelves as if whispering stories to one another. In the middle of the room stands a long oak table, smooth and shiny from hundreds of years of elbows, and beside it a squashy armchair with a patchwork quilt. The whole room smells of ink, beeswax candles and old paper, with a hint of cinnamon drifting up from the kitchen far below.

Why is it called the Library of Lost Winters? Because it remembers. Every winter that ever was, every snowfall, every frozen river, every story that people told by the fire and then forgot: the library keeps them all safe, in its books, so nothing is ever truly lost.
And the library doesn't only keep its memories in books.

Along one curved wall, on narrow shelves that climb almost to the ceiling, sit hundreds and hundreds of glass globes, each one about as big as a grapefruit, resting on a little wooden stand. These are the Storm Globes. Inside every one, a real winter storm from long ago is kept, tiny and safe behind the glass. Each stand has a small brass label. The Great Blizzard. The Winter of the Very Big Icicles. The Gentle Snow on the Night Snowbell Was Born.

When you pick up a Storm Globe and turn it slowly in your hands, the little storm inside wakes up. Snowflakes swirl. Wind whirls. Some globes hold fierce gray blizzards that spin and tumble. Some hold soft, sparkly snowfalls that drift down slow as feathers. One holds a pink sunrise over fresh snow, and one holds a night of falling stars. And if you hold a Storm Globe up to your ear, the way you'd listen to a seashell, you can hear the wind of that winter, whistling very, very softly, whoooooo, from far away and long ago.
Every storm that ever blew across the North Pole is kept here, so nobody ever forgets how each winter felt.

In one corner of the library there is a cozy reading nook, tucked under a window seat piled with pillows, where you can curl up with a book and a blanket while the snow falls outside. There is a giant old globe of the whole world that spins when you give it a push, whirrr, with the mountains raised up so you can feel them with your fingertips. There are wide, flat drawers full of maps that crinkle when you unfold them, and a wall of tiny wooden drawers, hundreds of them, each with a brass handle, holding cards that tell you where every single book can be found.
And the library has a keeper.
Santa! Mrs. Claus!
A small elf popped out from behind a tall stack of atlases. This was Snowbell, the librarian.

Snowbell is small, even for an elf. She has deep brown skin and two long silver-white braids that swing when she moves, and there are almost always little curls of paper caught in them. On her nose she wears spectacles made of frost-crystal, which sparkle when she reads and always sit a tiny bit crooked. She wears a cozy blue cardigan with deep pockets stuffed full of pencils, bookmarks and scraps of paper with notes on them. Like every elf, she has a bell on the tip of her knitted cap, but hers is wrapped in a little puff of wool, so that it goes plink instead of jingle and never disturbs anyone who is reading.
Snowbell's voice is soft, the way a librarian's voice should be, but bright, like a lantern. And more than anything in the world, Snowbell loves a mystery.
I heard about Blitzen,
she said.
The whole North Pole is talking about her. Not in a gossipy way. In a caring way.
She's healthy, Snowbell,
Santa said.
Strong heart, strong legs. But when she leaps for the sky, it's as if she can't quite remember how to meet the air.
Snowbell's face turned serious, the way it always did when a really good mystery walked through her door. She pushed her crooked spectacles up her nose.
Then we start the way we always start,
she said.
With questions.

She led them through the library, her soft slippers going pad, pad, pad on the wooden floor. They passed shelves of geography books with tiny maps painted on their spines. They passed a whole section about Arctic ice, its books cold to the touch. They passed a row of books about reindeer, decorated with little painted reindeer running along the spines, their antlers shining like starbursts.
There, Snowbell paused and tapped one of the books.
Did you know,
she said,

that reindeer can see colors that people can't? It's true. Reindeer can see ultraviolet light. To our eyes, the Arctic snow looks plain white. But to a reindeer, the snow, the lichen and the sky are full of patterns we will never see.
So reindeer may see things in the sky that we can't,
said Mrs. Claus slowly.
Exactly,
said Snowbell, and her spectacles sparkled.
Which is why we're not going to start with a book. We're going up.

At the back of the library, hidden behind a tall shelf of star charts, was a narrow little staircase that Santa had almost forgotten about. It curled upward like the inside of a seashell. Snowbell went first, her slippers going pad, pad, pad, then Mrs. Claus, then Santa, who had to tuck in his tummy and turn sideways in a few places. Ooof.
At the top, they stepped into the most magical room in the whole North Pole.

It was round and quiet, and its ceiling was one enormous dome of glass, like the inside of a giant snow globe. Right in the middle of the dome was a great round window, clearer than all the rest, called the Moon Window. Through it, you could see the whole night sky: the stars, the moon, and the northern lights swirling green and violet overhead.

All around the walls stood tall cabinets of pale birch wood with glass doors. And on their velvet-lined shelves, carefully arranged, row after row, were antlers. Hundreds of them. Small antlers and enormous ones, smooth ones and knobbly ones, some pale as cream and some brown as toffee. Beside each pair was a little card, written in neat elf handwriting, with a reindeer's name and the year.
The Antler Archive,
Snowbell said softly.

Every spring, the North Pole reindeer shed their antlers, and every year they grow brand new ones. The elves collect the old ones from the snow and bring them here, so we can remember every reindeer who ever lived at the North Pole.
She touched the glass gently.
They aren't trophies. They're records. Like a family photo album.

Snowbell walked along the cabinets until she came to the very oldest one, at the far end of the room. Inside, on a shelf all by itself, rested a single pair of antlers, silvery with age, so tall and so beautifully branched that they looked like a winter tree.
These belonged to Firstlight,
said Snowbell.
The very first reindeer who ever flew.
She smiled at Santa.
And Blitzen's great-great-great-grandmother, with more greats than anyone can count.
Mrs. Claus put her hand over her heart.
Blitzen's family,
she whispered.
All the way back to the very beginning.
Watch,
said Snowbell.

One by one, she turned down the lanterns, until the room was lit only by the northern lights, pouring down through the Moon Window. Ribbons of green and violet light fell softly across Firstlight's antlers.

And slowly, as if they were waking up, thin silver lines began to appear on the old antlers. They spread along every branch, curling and crossing, until the antlers were covered with tiny shining symbols.
Runes,
Santa breathed.
Reindeer Runes,
said Snowbell.
The oldest writing at the North Pole. They only show up in the light of the aurora, the northern lights. In lantern light, or even in moonlight, you'd never know they were there.
She leaned so close that her nose nearly touched the glass.

Flying reindeer carry the story of their lives on their antlers: where they've traveled, who they love, what they've learned. Nobody has been able to read them all for a thousand years. But we do know a few.

A rune is a special shape that stands for a word, like a little picture-letter. You already know some shapes like that. A heart shape can mean love. An arrow can mean this way. Reindeer Runes work the same way: each little shape means a word.
She pointed to three runes in a row, near the base of the antlers.
That one, a straight line standing all by itself, means Winter. This one, shaped like a little upside-down antler, means Root. And this one, pointing up like the top of a mountain, means Flight.
Winter. Root. Flight,
Mrs. Claus said slowly.
Flight… from a root?
But Santa was looking higher, at the very tip of the tallest branch. There, a row of runes glowed brighter than all the rest, silver-blue, and they looked very familiar.
Snowbell,
he said.
I've seen those runes before. On the spine of a book.
Snowbell gasped so loudly that the bell on her cap went plink.
The book that won't open!
she cried.
The one on the very top shelf. I've tried to open it for years and years, and it never budges. Its runes look exactly like those!

Then down they hurried, round and round the seashell stairs, back into the library. Snowbell scampered up a rolling ladder, all the way to the very top shelf, rumble, rumble, rumble, and reached into a shadowy corner. She pulled out a heavy book bound in deep blue leather. Silver runes glimmered along its spine, the very same runes they had just seen at the tip of Firstlight's antlers.
This one doesn't like just anyone opening it,
she said, hugging the book to her chest as she slid back down the ladder. Whoosh.
But I think it will put up with you.
She set it on the long oak table beneath the arched window. Outside, the northern lights rippled closer, as if leaning in to watch.
Mrs. Claus brushed a thin dusting of frost from the cover. It felt cold and smooth under her fingers, like a frozen pond.
Vetrarblómssaga,
she read.
The Saga of Winter's Bloom.
Nobody has opened that one in five hundred years,
said Santa.
That's because it only glows when it wants to be read,
said Snowbell.
And just then, as if it had been waiting for exactly the right moment, the runes on the cover began to glow, soft silver-blue, like moonlight on snow.
Mrs. Claus smiled.
Some things only open when the time is just right,
she said softly.

She lifted the heavy cover. The pages fluttered, flip, flip, flip, as though a breeze no one else could feel was turning them. Then they settled on two pages decorated in shining silver ink, with tiny painted snowflakes and flowers curling around the edges. At the top, a title curled like frost on a window: The Winterbreath Verse.
Mrs. Claus read it aloud. Her voice became soft and slow, the way you might sing a lullaby:

Beneath the hush of northern night,
Where snow remembers silver light,
Five winter blooms in secret keep
The dream of sky where reindeer leap.

One stirs the breath of hidden streams,
A pale fire kept in frostbound dreams;
One wakes the glow where shadows lie,
A lantern made of lullaby.

One guards the roots where forest sleeps,
Its petals warm the dark it keeps;
One hums where ancient winds arise,
A song that threads through frozen skies.

And one—a star in winter's palm—
Holds joy enough to summon calm,
For when its silent fragrance flows,
The heart of Christmas softly grows.

When Earth gives voice beneath the snow,
And Sky sends down its wandering glow,
Their meeting stirs the northern tide
Where hoof and hope together ride.

For in that place where light takes flight,
And mycel threads remember night,
The world renews its gentle art—
To lift the weary, warm the heart.

Seek not to claim what winter sows;
The bloom will come when kindness grows.
Walk soft, breathe deep, let wonder guide—
And joy will find the ones who ride.

When Mrs. Claus finished, the last lines shimmered on the page, as if someone had breathed on them very gently. For a moment, nobody spoke. The copper pipes chimed, tink, tinkle. A lantern flickered. Somewhere far below, a clock struck the hour, bong, bong.

Then Mrs. Claus noticed something she hadn't seen at first. In the margin of the page, beside five of the lines, the ones that began One…, someone long ago had drawn five tiny runes in silver ink. Each one was different. None of them were runes that Snowbell knew.
Five runes for five blooms,
Snowbell whispered, pushing her spectacles up her nose.
And I can't read a single one of them.
At the very bottom of the page, where the parchment had worn thin, there might once have been one more mark. But it was far too faded to see.
Five winter blooms,
Mrs. Claus whispered at last.
Five flowers, in five special places. And a way to help what's fading.
Then she noticed something peeking out from between the pages: the end of a silver cord.

She gave it the gentlest tug, and out slid a scroll, rolled up tight and tied with that shining cord. The paper was thick and creamy, soft as felt, and it smelled of cedar wood and something sweet, like dried flowers. Mrs. Claus untied the cord and unrolled the scroll on the oak table. Snowbell held down one end, and Santa held down the other.

Across the top of the scroll, someone long ago had painted five flowers, very carefully, with tiny brushstrokes. They looked so real that you almost expected them to sway in a breeze. At the very bottom, the paper had gone brown and soft with age, and if anything had ever been painted there, it had faded away long ago.
The first was a pink flower shaped like a little slipper, with a fuzzy yellow patch, as if a fairy had dropped her shoe in the moss.
The second was a pale pink star with a frilly white lip, rising from a little cone-shaped bulb, like a flower waking up from a long nap.
The third was a tiny violet lantern, no bigger than your fingertip.
The fourth was a cluster of ghost-white bells, as white as fresh snow.
And the fifth was not a flower at all, but a dark green leaf, netted all over with fine silver lines, like a map of tiny rivers.

And in the middle of the scroll was a map of the whole wide world, with a thin silver dotted line winding from one flower to the next, like a trail of tiny footprints. Each flower sat beside the place where it grows. A spruce forest in the far north. The snowy roof of the world. A mossy waterfall in the mountains. A rainforest of giant trees. And a cedar valley, deep in the mountains.

Mrs. Claus took out her sketchbook and turned to the very last page, where her unfinished pencil drawing waited without any color. She held it next to the first painting on the scroll, the little pink slipper. They were the very same flower.
Mrs. Claus looked from her sketch to the painting and back again. Then her eyes went wide.
Kris, I know this flower,
she whispered.
I've been drawing her for years, from a picture in an old book. She's an orchid. She's the one I've always wanted to see.

Slowly, she looked at the other four paintings, one by one. The pale pink star rising from its little cone-shaped bulb. The tiny violet lantern. The ghost-white bells. The silver-veined leaf. Some of them she had seen in books. Some she had never seen in her whole life. But the more she looked, the brighter her eyes grew.
I think these are orchids too,
she said.
All five of them. Five winter blooms.
She looked up at Santa.
The verse was talking about orchids all along.
Santa let out a long, wondering breath.
Snow orchids,
he said softly.
Snowbell's spectacles sparkled so brightly that they nearly glowed.
The Winterbreath Verse tells us how to go,
Mrs. Claus said softly.
Gently, and with kindness. And this map shows us where.
But the scroll didn't tell them everything. It didn't say what each orchid had to teach, or why they needed all five, or what any of it had to do with Blitzen.
I suppose,
said Santa, stroking his beard,
we'll just have to go and ask them.

All around the edges of the scroll ran rows of little runes. As they watched, the runes shimmered silver, then dimmed, then shimmered again, like the slow blink of a sleepy star. They were the same runes that had glowed on Firstlight's antlers, the ones they could read and the many they couldn't yet.
Winter. Root. Flight,
Snowbell whispered, finding the three runes she knew.
And all the rest still waiting to be read.
Mrs. Claus traced one of the runes with her fingertip. It felt faintly warm, like a mug that has just been put down.
If nobody can read all the runes,
she said softly,
then maybe the orchids will teach us.
She looked out the arched window at the dancing lights.

You know, Kris, the world has been a little mixed up lately. Some flowers wake up too early in spring, and some birds arrive a little late. The seasons have been wobbling, the way a spinning top wobbles. Maybe Blitzen is feeling a wobble too. And orchids are very good at noticing when things change.
Then we must find them,
said Santa.
Mrs. Claus nodded.
And we go gently,
she said.

Seek not to claim what winter sows. We won't pick them, and we won't dig them up. We'll visit, we'll listen, and we'll only take what they are ready to give: a breath of scent, a drop of water, a leaf that has already let go.
Santa stood up and straightened his red coat, and a twinkle crept back into his eye.
You know, some people say I'm only make-believe,
he said.
But a story is just a truth wearing a costume. And between you and me…
He patted his round tummy.
I look very good in red.
Snowbell laughed so hard that her spectacles fogged right over, and she had to wipe them on her cardigan.

The three of them stayed up late into the night at the long oak table, planning their journey. Snowbell hurried back and forth with armfuls of atlases and old travel journals, their covers worn soft as mittens. Mrs. Claus spread the maps out flat and drew tiny symbols on them with her colored pencils: a pink slipper, a pale pink star, a violet lantern, a white bell and a silver-veined leaf. Santa held the lantern and watched their path take shape, winding across the whole wide world.

It was Mrs. Claus who noticed the tiny snowflakes. Beside every one of the five flower paintings on the scroll, someone had drawn a little snowflake turning into a drop of water, as if it were melting.
Oh,
she said softly.
Look, Kris. They bloom where the snow says goodbye. Each one in her own place, right beside the melting snow, at her very own time.
She ran her finger along the silver dotted line.
The first won't bloom until the snow melts in Lapland, at the end of spring. Then the others, one by one, all through the summer. We'll have to follow the melting snow around the world.
Santa was quiet for a moment. Then he nodded slowly.
Then we'll wait for each one,
he said.
Some things can't be hurried. Not even by Santa.
And Blitzen will wait with us,
said Snowbell softly.

An elf from the kitchen brought up a tray of hot spiced apple cider and a plate of warm ginger cookies that crunched at the edges and stayed soft in the middle. Snowbell nibbled hers in tiny bites, so the crumbs wouldn't fall on the books.
We'll need warm clothes,
said Mrs. Claus, ticking things off on her fingers.
And sketchbooks, and good boots, and plenty of oat-and-berry cakes.
Kindness always travels best with a little sweetness,
Santa agreed.

Before they left, Snowbell handed Mrs. Claus a fresh sheet of parchment. On it, the words of the Winterbreath Verse were appearing all by themselves, one letter at a time, in Mrs. Claus's very own handwriting.
Take it with you,
Snowbell said.
It seems to like you.

As they went down the twisty stairs, the Library of Lost Winters gave a long, happy sigh, hhhhhhh, the way a cat sighs when it curls up by the fire. Another story had just begun, and the library would remember it.

That night, after the big house had gone quiet and everyone was tucked in bed, Mrs. Claus could not sleep. She thought of Blitzen, alone in the dark barn, trying so hard to fly. So she pulled on her cranberry cloak, lit her lantern, and tiptoed back out through the snow. Crunch, crunch, crunch.

The barn was dim and hushed. The other reindeer were fast asleep, curled up in the straw with their noses tucked into their warm fur, breathing slow and deep. Hhhhh. Hhhhh. Little Lilt was snoring the tiniest snore. But Blitzen was awake. She was lying in her stall with her head low, gazing up at the northern lights through the high window.

Mrs. Claus sat down in the straw beside her. It was soft and prickly and smelled of summer fields. She hung her lantern on a beam, so it made a little circle of gold around them both, and she stroked the soft fur between Blitzen's ears.
Then she began to sing, softly and slowly, the way she had sung to every newborn reindeer calf for years and years.

By the last verse, Blitzen's eyes had slowly closed, and her breathing had become slow and deep and peaceful. Hhhhh. Hhhhh. Mrs. Claus left the lantern glowing on the beam, so that if Blitzen woke in the night, there would be a warm little light beside her.
Back at the big house, Santa was waiting in his armchair by the fire, with his slippers on and his feet stretched toward the crackling flames. Pop, crackle, pop.
You sang to her,
he said, with a gentle smile.
I did, Kris,
said Mrs. Claus, warming her cold hands by the fire.
She needed to know she's loved on the ground, too. Not only when she flies.
Santa reached over and squeezed her hand. Outside, the northern lights drifted slowly across the sky, soft and sleepy now, as if they were tucking the whole North Pole into bed.

Upstairs, the scroll lay rolled up safe on the nightstand, tied with its silver cord. In the barn, the lantern glowed beside a sleeping reindeer. And everyone at the North Pole, from the smallest elf to Santa himself, drifted off to sleep knowing one thing: when the snow began to melt at the edges of the world, the journey would begin.
Weeks went by.

Then, one day in the middle of March, something wonderful happened at the North Pole. A thin line of gold appeared at the edge of the sky, then a sliver of orange, and then, for the first time in six whole months, the sun peeked up over the edge of the world. The elves ran out into the snow, cheering and waving their caps, jingle, jingle, jingle. Every day after that, the sun climbed a little higher, until it didn't set at all, and the North Pole glowed all day and all night long.

All that time, Blitzen rested. Mrs. Claus visited her every evening, and Starbloom and little Lilt kept her company. And every day, Mrs. Claus unrolled the scroll and looked at the little painting of the pink slipper.

In the spring, Blitzen's old antlers loosened and fell off, one and then the other, clunk and clunk, into the straw. It didn't hurt her one bit. All reindeer shed their antlers every year. The elves carried them carefully up the seashell stairs to the Antler Archive, and gave them a little card of their own. And right away, Blitzen began to grow new ones: two soft, fuzzy little knobs at first, covered in a velvety brown skin, that grew a little bigger every single day.
Then, one bright morning near the end of May, the Reindeer Rune beside the slipper painting began to glow, soft and silver-blue. Far away in Lapland, the snow was melting.
It was time.
That morning, the whole village was busy getting the sleigh ready for a very special trip.

Santa's sleigh is a beautiful thing. It is made of polished wood the color of honey, carved all over with snowflakes and, if you look closely, tiny orchids that Mrs. Claus asked the elves to add. Its long runners curl up at the front like the top of a candy cane, and its seat is cushioned in soft red velvet, with a thick wool blanket folded on top. On the back hangs a row of silver bells that ring whenever it moves. Jingle, jingle.

The elves bustled back and forth with their arms full, their cap bells jingling. They packed warm scarves and mittens, sketchbooks and colored pencils, a coil of climbing rope, a little glass dish for looking closely at tiny things, a basket of oat-and-berry cakes, and a few jars of golden honey from Mrs. Claus's greenhouse bees.

But this trip would be different from Christmas Eve. On Christmas Eve, Santa's sleigh is piled high with toys for every child in the world, so heavy that it takes the whole team of reindeer to pull it. This time, the sleigh would carry only Santa, Mrs. Claus, a basket of cakes and a few sketchbooks. So only four reindeer would go: Dasher, the fastest of all; twirling Dancer; clever, curious Vixen, who sniffed every bag as the elves buckled on her harness; and quick, sparkly Comet.

The others would stay home with Blitzen, so she would never be alone. Prancer, Cupid and Donner would keep up their practice flights every evening. Evenstar, the wise old leader, would watch over the whole herd. Gentle Starbloom would keep Blitzen company in her stall. And little Lilt, who was too young for such a long journey, would stay too, which made her ears droop for only a moment, until Blitzen nuzzled her.
And they would fly the way Santa's reindeer always fly: along the auroral road.

That is the great secret of reindeer flight. To us, the northern lights look like beautiful ribbons of color in the sky. But to Santa's reindeer, they are a road, a glowing path they can feel tingling through their hooves, and they run along it, up and up, into the sky. Even in places where people can't see the northern lights at all, far to the south, or in the bright daytime, the auroral road is still there, faint and hidden, the way the stars are still in the sky during the day even though we can't see them. The reindeer can always feel it. And with their special eyes, perhaps they can even see it.

On the auroral road, faraway places come close together, and you can cross the whole world in a few heartbeats. That's how Santa visits every home in one night. And that's how this little sleigh would reach five orchids on the far sides of the world.

When everything was ready, the four reindeer lifted their heads, and their hooves began to tingle. Even in the bright summer sunshine, where nobody else could see it, they could feel the auroral road, humming softly, like the strings of a harp touched by light.

Santa climbed into the sleigh and took the reins in his big mittened hands. Mrs. Claus climbed in beside him and tucked the wool blanket over their knees. Then she leaned over the side and spoke to Evenstar.
Keep watch over her for us,
she said softly.
Evenstar dipped her silvery head, as if to say, Of course I will.
Blitzen stepped up to the sleigh and gently rested her nose in Mrs. Claus's hands. Her breath was warm and smelled of hay. She understood. She always did.

All along the snowy lane, the elves had lined up to say goodbye, waving their caps and ringing little hand bells, so the whole lane twinkled and jingled. Evenstar stood tall in the sunshine. Little Lilt tilted her big ears toward a song only she could hear. And in the barn doorway, Blitzen lifted her head to watch.
Then the elves began to sing them on their way.
When the last note of the song had floated away, Santa gave the reins a gentle shake.
Here we go,
he said.

Dasher, Dancer, Vixen and Comet leaped forward together, their feet going click, click, click, and then their hooves lifted off the snow. The sleigh began to rise behind them, slowly at first, then faster, up and up, past the snowy rooftops and the smoking chimneys and the glowing arched window of the library. The waving elves shrank to tiny colorful dots below. Mrs. Claus waved and waved until she couldn't see Blitzen anymore.
Then the reindeer ran onto the auroral road. And here is a secret: for those who travel on it, the road always shows its colors, even in the brightest daylight.

All around them, ribbons of green and violet and pink swirled and floated, soft as silk scarves, close enough to touch. The air hummed with a sound like a faraway choir. The sleigh bells chimed. And the whole world below seemed to fold up gently, like a map, so that faraway places came close together.

Then Mrs. Claus noticed something else. In the shimmering light of the auroral road, faint silver lines had begun to glow on Dasher's antlers, and on Dancer's, Vixen's and Comet's too. Tiny runes, curling along every branch, just like the ones on Firstlight's antlers in the Moon Window.
Kris,
she said slowly.
Their antlers. The runes are showing.
Santa looked, and his face grew thoughtful.
Every flying reindeer carries them,
he said.
The story of her life, written in light.
Then he was quiet for a moment.
Last winter, under the northern lights, I looked at Blitzen's antlers. They were dark, Linnea. Not a single rune was glowing.
Mrs. Claus held her sketchbook tight.
Then that's part of what we need to find,
she said softly.
Whatever made her runes go dark.

Their first stop was already glowing ahead of them: Lapland, a land of snowy forests and frozen lakes at the very top of Europe, where reindeer have lived alongside people for thousands of years. It was the land where Mrs. Claus had grown up as a little girl. And long ago, the scientist Carl Linnaeus had traveled there too, exploring its forests and collecting its flowers, on one of the most famous journeys of his life.
Somewhere in those quiet spruce forests, beneath the trees, the little pink Fairy Slipper Orchid was waiting, patient as winter.
Mrs. Claus held her sketchbook tight against her chest, right over her silver twinflower brooch.
The journey had begun.
The four reindeer glided down out of the northern lights, pulling the sleigh behind them as softly as a feather.

Back at the North Pole, the snow would lie deep on the sea ice for many weeks yet. But here in Lapland, far to the south, spring had come at last. The long winter snow was finally melting, and the whole forest was waking up.
The sleigh landed with a soft whumph in a little clearing, and Santa and Mrs. Claus climbed out and looked around.

They were standing in a forest of tall, dark spruce trees, so tall that they had to tip their heads all the way back to see the tops. The trees stood in long rows like the pillars of a great green cathedral, and the sunlight slanted between them in long golden beams, full of drifting sparkles of pollen. Here and there, old patches of snow still lay in the shadows, melting slowly. Drip. Drip. Trickle. Little streams of meltwater ran under the moss, gurgling softly where you couldn't see them.

And the moss! It covered everything, the ground and the rocks and the fallen logs, thick and green and springy, like the softest carpet in the world. When Mrs. Claus stepped onto it, her little red boot sank right down, squish.

The air smelled of pine sap and wet earth and melting snow. From somewhere deep in the woods, a cuckoo called, cuck-oo, cuck-oo. And far away, faintly, came the gentle clink, clonk of a bell. It was a reindeer bell, worn by the reindeer of the Sámi people, who have herded reindeer in these northern lands for a very, very long time.
Mrs. Claus took a deep breath, and her eyes shone.
I walked these woods when I was a little girl,
she said softly.
Every summer, twinflowers bloom all along these paths, two little pink bells on every stem.
She touched the silver twinflower brooch on her cloak.
I never dreamed I'd come back looking for an orchid.
Santa unrolled the scroll. Beside the little painting of the pink slipper, one of the Reindeer Runes was glowing softly, silver-blue. It was one they couldn't read yet.
I think that means she's close,
whispered Mrs. Claus.

They walked slowly between the trees, side by side. Finding an orchid is not like finding a red ball in the snow. You have to go slowly. You have to look carefully, low down, in all the little hollows and shadows. Mrs. Claus knelt every few steps, gently parting the moss with her fingers. Santa peered behind fallen logs. They passed low bushes of wild blueberries, which were just beginning to flower, covered in tiny pink-and-white bells.
The Fairy Slipper always blooms when the blueberries do,
Mrs. Claus whispered.
We must be close.
Then, beside an old spruce log covered in moss, she stopped very, very still.
Kris,
she breathed.
Look.
There, standing all alone in the moss, was a single small flower on a single slender stem, about as tall as your hand.
It was the Fairy Slipper.
Her scientific name is Calypso bulbosa,
Mrs. Claus whispered.

Say it with me: kuh-LIP-so bul-BO-suh. Calypso was a sea nymph in a very old Greek story, and the name means 'the hidden one,' because this little orchid hides deep in the forest. Bulbosa means 'with a bulb,' for the little round bulb, called a corm, tucked under the moss. And the very first scientist to describe her was Carl Linnaeus himself, the botanist I was named after.
Santa bent down and counted softly.
Three sepals and two petals, all narrow and pink, pointing up like a crown. And the third petal must be that little slipper. Her lip!
Exactly,
said Mrs. Claus, beaming.
The bumblebee lands right there.

At the top, five narrow pink-purple petals stretched upward and outward, like the points of a little crown, or ribbons streaming in the wind. Beneath them hung the most wonderful part: a little pouch shaped exactly like a tiny slipper, the kind a fairy might wear to a ball. The front of the slipper was creamy white, sprinkled with pink-purple spots, and right in the middle sat a fuzzy tuft of bright yellow hairs, soft as a baby chick. Inside the slipper ran stripes of reddish brown, like the lines on a seashell. And when Mrs. Claus bent close, she smelled something sweet and warm, like vanilla.
At the bottom of the stem lay one single leaf, flat on the moss, green on top and a deep reddish purple underneath.

For a long moment, Mrs. Claus didn't say anything at all. Then, very slowly, she took out her sketchbook and turned to the last page, to the pencil drawing she had never colored in. She took out her colored pencils, one at a time. Pink for the crown of petals. Creamy white and purple dots for the slipper. Yellow for the fuzzy tuft. Reddish brown for the stripes.
And at last, after all those years, she colored it in.
Now I know,
she whispered.
Now I know what colors she really is.
Underneath, in small, neat letters, she wrote her first field note of the journey:
Fairy Slipper. Growing alone in deep moss beside a fallen spruce, blooming with the blueberries. One flower, one leaf. Smells of vanilla.
Santa knelt beside her in the moss, being very careful where he put his big boots.
She's so small,
he said.
How does something this tiny live through a whole Lapland winter, buried under all that snow?
By storing the sun,
said Mrs. Claus. She pointed to the single leaf.

That leaf grew last autumn. It stayed green under the snow all winter long, like a little solar panel waiting in the dark. And under the ground, she has a tiny round bulb, about the size of a pea, packed with food she made from last year's sunshine. She saves summer light inside herself and lives on it through the dark months.
And by belonging to this place,
said a soft little voice.
Santa and Mrs. Claus turned around.

Sitting on the mossy spruce log was the tiniest person they had ever seen. She was exactly as tall as the Fairy Slipper itself. Her skin was smooth and pale like birch bark, with little dark markings here and there, just like a birch tree. Her hair was soft and gray-green and curly, made of lichen. On her back were two thin wings that shimmered green and gold, like a dragonfly's, and when she moved them, they made a tiny sound, frrrrr. Her eyes were the warm brown of forest soil, and her voice was as soft as a dewdrop landing on a leaf.
She was the Guardian of the Fairy Slipper.
Welcome, Santa Claus,
she said.
Welcome, Linnea, who draws what she does not take. You've come for the Snow Orchids.
Santa bowed low, so low that his beard brushed the moss.
We have,
he said.
One of our reindeer, Blitzen, has lost her harmony with the sky. We're hoping the orchids can help us understand why.
The guardian nodded slowly.
Then the first thing you must understand,
she said,
is the most important thing of all. No orchid lives alone.
She fluttered down from the log, frrrrr, and landed in the moss beside the Fairy Slipper.
Look below,

she said, and she lifted a corner of moss, very gently, like lifting a blanket. Underneath, threading through the dark soil, were fine white strands, thinner than the thinnest hair, branching and crossing like a tiny net.

These are her fungus friends. My Fairy Slipper's seeds are smaller than specks of dust, so small that they carry no food of their own. They can't sprout by themselves at all. These threads find them, and feed them, and help them grow. Without the fungus, there would be no Fairy Slipper. Not a single one.
Mrs. Claus nodded.
The helpers you can't see,
she said softly.
Just then, there was a deep, fuzzy humming sound. Bzzzzzzzz.

A big, round bumblebee came bumbling between the trees, striped black and golden yellow, as plump as a little teddy bear. She circled the Fairy Slipper once, twice, then landed right on the slipper's fuzzy yellow tuft and crawled inside.
And look above,
whispered the guardian.

That's a young queen bumblebee. She has only just woken up from her long winter sleep under the ground, and she's very hungry. Here is a secret: my Fairy Slipper has no sweet nectar to give her. But she looks as if she does, with her bright pink petals, her vanilla smell, and that yellow tuft that looks just like pollen. So the young queen comes to check.
The bumblebee backed out of the slipper and buzzed away toward the blueberry bushes. On her fuzzy back, if you looked very closely, were two tiny yellow specks.
Those are pollen packets,
the guardian said.

She'll carry them to the next Fairy Slipper she visits, and then that flower can make seeds. The bee doesn't mind. She soon learns where the real nectar is, in the blueberry flowers, and she has a feast there.

But Mrs. Claus had already turned to a fresh page in her sketchbook, and her pencil was flying. She drew the bumblebee as quickly and carefully as she could, before it was gone: the round, fuzzy body, the stripes of black and golden yellow, the see-through wings, and, on its back, two tiny dots of pollen. Then she colored it in and wrote underneath, in small, neat letters:
Queen bumblebee. Just awake from winter. Visited the Fairy Slipper, found no nectar, left carrying two pollen packets. Flew to the blueberry flowers.
Now I have both of them,
she said happily.
The orchid, and her partner.
A fungus below and a bee above,
said Santa slowly.
And the trees, and the moss, and the snow that melts at just the right time.
Just so,
said the guardian. Then her small face became a little serious.

Lately, the world's rhythms have been shifting. Some springs come too early, some too late. Sometimes the bees wake up before the flowers are ready, or the flowers bloom before the bees are awake. When the timing is out of tune, everything that depends on it feels the wobble.
Like Blitzen,
said Mrs. Claus quietly.
Like Blitzen,
agreed the guardian.
But a wobble is not an ending. Things that are connected can help each other find the rhythm again. That is what partners are for.
Mrs. Claus knelt in the moss.
We don't want to take anything that the Fairy Slipper needs,
she said.
Her flower must stay. Her leaf must stay. Her bulb must stay.
The guardian smiled, pleased.
That is wise. Then I will give you something she can spare.
She fluttered to the Fairy Slipper and floated beside its lip.
Breathe in,
she said. Mrs. Claus knelt down in the moss and breathed in very gently, and there it was: the faintest sweet scent, like vanilla and spring rain.
My Fairy Slipper's sweet scent is how she calls the bumblebees to her,
said the guardian.
One breath of it is all she can spare, and all you will need.
She cupped her tiny hands in the air above the flower, and a little glimmer, no bigger than a dewdrop, floated up between her fingers.

Mrs. Claus unstoppered a little glass bottle, no bigger than her thumb, and the glimmer drifted inside. She pressed the cork in tight, and on its paper label she wrote, in her neatest handwriting: Fairy Slipper. Patience and stored light. Nothing had been taken from the flower, not even a petal.

Then it was her turn to give a gift. Mrs. Claus never takes anything from a wild place without leaving something behind, and her gift is always the same. She opened the little glass door of her aurora lantern, the one that lights her greenhouse, and out floated a single drop of northern light, green and pink and shimmering. It drifted down and settled on the Fairy Slipper's leaf like a tiny star. For a moment it glowed. Then it soaked softly into the leaf and was gone, leaving nothing behind at all.
Thank you for teaching us,
Mrs. Claus whispered. In a wild place, a gift that leaves no trace is the very best kind.
A true gift,
said the guardian, and her wings went frrrrr with happiness.

As Santa and Mrs. Claus walked back to the sleigh, the sun was sinking low and gold between the trees. But it didn't set. In Lapland in late spring, the sun barely sets at all. It just slides along the edge of the sky all night long, painting everything in soft pink and gold.
One orchid,
Mrs. Claus said, holding her sketchbook close.
And one lesson.
She opened her sketchbook to look at her drawing one more time, and suddenly she stopped walking.

She had drawn the Fairy Slipper's flower from the side: the little slipper-shaped lip, round like a tiny cup, with its fuzzy beard of yellow hairs inside and two tiny horns underneath, and above it all, her petals sweeping up and over like a crown. And all together, those lines made a shape. A shape she had seen before.
Kris,
she whispered.
It's a rune.

With trembling fingers, she unfolded her copy of the Winterbreath Verse and ran her finger down the margin. There, beside the lines And one—a star in winter's palm— / Holds joy enough to summon calm, / For when its silent fragrance flows, was the very same rune: a little slipper-shaped cup with a tuft inside and two tiny horns below, under a sweeping crown.
A star with a sweet, silent fragrance,
said Mrs. Claus.
That's the Fairy Slipper. And this rune means…
She thought of the little bulb under the moss, holding last summer's light, waiting patiently all winter under the snow for this one moment to bloom.
Wait.
Santa unrolled the scroll. The rune beside the painting of the pink slipper had stopped glowing. It shone steady and silver now, as if it were saying, Yes. You've learned me.
Mrs. Claus drew the rune carefully at the bottom of her page and wrote beside it: Wait.
Santa nodded.
Patience,
he said.
Trusting what you've stored up inside, even in the dark. And never forgetting that nobody does it alone.
He thought of Blitzen, far away in the barn, and he hoped, somehow, that she could feel it too.

They climbed into the sleigh, and Santa gave the reins a gentle shake. Dasher, Dancer, Vixen and Comet tossed their antlers and leaped, and up they rose, jingle, jingle, over the spruce tops and the blueberry bushes and the little clearing where a tiny guardian stood waving. Then the northern lights folded around them once more, green and violet and pink, and carried them away toward the next orchid, half a world away, where the mountains are so high that they touch the clouds.
Up and away flew the sleigh, along the shining auroral road.

Mrs. Claus snuggled under the wool blanket and peeked over the side. Far, far below, the world rolled past like a giant painted map. First came the dark green forests of the north, so big that they went on and on, farther than anyone could ever walk. Then wide rivers, winding and glinting like silver ribbons dropped on the ground. Then golden grasslands, rippling in the wind like the fur of an enormous sleeping cat. Then a great sandy desert, with dunes that rose and fell like frozen ocean waves, glowing orange and pink in the evening light.

The wind rushed past, cool and fresh, and tugged at Santa's beard and Mrs. Claus's braid. Whoosh. The sleigh bells jingled. Comet's ears flicked forward with excitement, and Dasher kept trying to race the wind the whole way.
Kris,
said Mrs. Claus, pointing.
Look ahead.
Far away, at the very edge of the sky, something white was shining. At first it looked like a row of clouds. But as they flew closer and closer, Mrs. Claus gasped. They weren't clouds at all.
They were mountains.

They were the biggest mountains she had ever seen, so tall that their tops poked right up through the clouds, sharp and white and glittering with snow and ice. There wasn't just one. There were dozens and dozens of them, a whole wall of mountains stretching across the bottom of the sky, as far as she could see to the left and as far as she could see to the right.
The Himalayas,
said Santa softly.
The tallest mountains in the whole world.

The sleigh glided between the great peaks. Up close, the mountains were even more amazing. Their sides were steep cliffs of gray stone streaked with white, and long rivers of ice, called glaciers, crept slowly down between them, blue-white and cracked like broken sugar. The air up here was so clear that every single rock seemed sharp, and the sky was the deepest blue that Mrs. Claus had ever seen, almost purple at the top.

Below the snowy peaks, the mountains were green. There were steep hillsides carved into little steps, where farmers grew their crops, like a giant green staircase. There were forests clinging to the slopes. And here and there, tucked into the valleys, were little villages of stone houses with colorful wooden windows.
Santa looked at the scroll. The rune beside the painting of the pale pink star-shaped flower was glowing softly, silver-blue.
Down there,
he said.
Near that village.
Hold on tight!
Santa called, and he gave the reins a gentle pull.

The four reindeer tipped their noses down, and the sleigh swooped lower and lower, past the clouds, whoosh, and down toward a small, flat, grassy field at the edge of a mountain village. Dasher's hooves touched the ground first, of course, thump, then Comet's and Dancer's and Vixen's, thump, thump, thump, and the sleigh slid to a stop on the soft grass with a gentle shhhhhh.
Santa climbed out of the sleigh and stretched his arms way up high. Then he took a big breath, and blinked in surprise.
Goodness,
he puffed.
The air feels thin up here.
It is thin,
said Mrs. Claus, a little out of breath herself.
We're so high up that there's less air to breathe. We'll have to walk slowly, and rest often.
The reindeer didn't seem to mind one bit. They shook their antlers and sniffed the cool mountain breeze, which smelled of snow and grass and woodsmoke.
And then, from across the field, came a deep, rumbly sound. Hrrrumph. Hrrrumph.

A group of enormous, shaggy animals was ambling toward them. They had long, thick hair that hung almost to the ground, like great big walking rugs, and curved horns, and bushy tails that swished from side to side. Some were black, some were brown, and one was white with black patches. Some were true yaks, and some were zopkyo, a cross between a yak and a cow, which are happier lower down the mountain, where it is warmer.
Yaks!
laughed Mrs. Claus.
The biggest yak walked right up to Vixen, and curious Vixen stretched out her neck until they were nose to nose. Hrrrumph, said the yak.
Hmmf, snorted Vixen politely.
The yak seemed to think about this. Then it grunted again, in what sounded like a very friendly way, and went back to munching grass.

Now a little boy came running across the field, waving his arms, and behind him came his mother, his father and his grandmother, all smiling. They were Sherpa people. Nepal is home to many different peoples, with many different languages, and the Sherpa are one of them. Sherpa families have lived high in these mountains for hundreds of years, and they know them better than almost anyone in the world. The boy wore a thick woolen hat with ear flaps, and his cheeks were rosy from the wind.
Namaste!
said the grandmother, pressing her hands together in front of her heart and bowing her head. It is a way of saying hello, and it means, more or less, I greet the goodness in you.
Namaste,
said Santa and Mrs. Claus, pressing their hands together and bowing back.

The Sherpa family invited them into their home, a sturdy little house with thick stone walls and a wooden door painted with bright flowers. Inside, it was warm and smoky and cozy. A fire crackled in a clay stove, and copper pots shone on the shelves. The grandmother poured them each a cup of hot tea from a tall wooden churn.
Mrs. Claus took a sip, and her eyebrows went up in surprise. The tea wasn't sweet at all. It was salty and buttery and creamy, almost like soup, and it warmed her all the way down to her toes.
Butter tea,
said the father, smiling.
Tea, salt, and butter from our animals' milk. Up here in the cold, it keeps you warm and strong.
It's wonderful,
said Mrs. Claus, and she meant it.

Then Mrs. Claus opened her basket. She had packed it at the North Pole before they left, because you never know whose kitchen you might end up sitting in. She gave the grandmother a jar of golden honey and a tin of her very best cookies, and she gave the little boy a gingerbread reindeer with white icing antlers. The boy's eyes went wide, and he held it so carefully that it looked as if he might never eat it at all.
The grandmother held the honey up to the window so that the light shone through it like amber, and smiled.
Thank you,

she said. Then she set out steaming bowls of dal bhat, rice with a warm lentil soup, and everyone ate together around the crackling stove, while the father told them about the mountain, and which slopes melt first in spring, and where the streams run.
When she showed the family the painting of the little pale flower on the scroll, the grandmother's face lit up. She pointed up the mountain, toward a forest just below the snow.
Up there,
she said.
On the mossy rocks, where the snow is going away. It blooms every year when the snow melts. A little pink star.
The boy wanted to come along too, but his mother laughed and said he had chores to do. So he waved goodbye from the doorway until they were out of sight.

The path up the mountain was narrow and rocky, and it zigzagged back and forth, back and forth, because the mountain was much too steep to climb straight up. Santa and Mrs. Claus walked slowly, crunch, crunch, over the little stones, stopping often to catch their breath. The reindeer stayed behind in the field to rest and nibble grass, keeping the yaks company.

All along the path, strings of little flags fluttered in the wind, stretched from rock to rock and from pole to pole. There were hundreds of them, in five bright colors: blue, white, red, green and yellow, over and over again. They snapped and flapped in the breeze, flap-flap-flap, like a crowd of happy birds.
Those are prayer flags,
said Mrs. Claus.
People here hang them so the wind will carry their kind wishes across the mountains, to everyone and everything. For peace, and good health, and happiness.
Santa watched the flags dancing.
So every time the wind blows,
he said,
it carries kindness everywhere.
Just so,
said Mrs. Claus.

They passed big flat stones carved with beautiful curly letters and painted in bright colors. The Sherpa grandmother had told them that, out of respect, travelers always walk to the left of these stones, keeping them on their right, so Santa and Mrs. Claus were careful to do the same.

Higher up, the path entered a forest of twisty old trees, and here Mrs. Claus stopped and clapped her hands in delight. The trees were covered in flowers. Big, round bunches of flowers, red as strawberries and pink as bubblegum, so many that the whole forest seemed to glow.
Rhododendrons!
she cried.
In some places, they grow as tall as houses.

The fallen petals made a soft pink carpet on the path. A little stream tumbled beside them over the rocks, so cold and clear that it looked like liquid glass, splish, splash, gurgle. And from a pile of stones nearby came a tiny squeak, eeep!, and a little round furry face peeked out. It looked a bit like a hamster with very round ears.
A pika,
whispered Mrs. Claus.
A little cousin of the rabbit.
The pika looked at them with bright black eyes, twitched its whiskers, and then scurried away with a mouthful of grass to store in its den for winter.

Higher and higher they climbed, into the oldest part of the forest. Here the rhododendron trees were gnarled and twisty, and their trunks and branches were wrapped in thick, soft cushions of green moss. The air grew colder, and Santa's breath came out in little white puffs again. And then, at last, they came to a place where the snow of winter still lay in the deep shade beneath the trees, slowly melting.

It was a magical place. On one side, the snow still lay deep and white and sparkling. On the other side, where it had melted, the ground was wet and dark and green, and little streams of meltwater trickled over the rocks, drip, drip, trickle. Right along the edge, where the white met the green, it was as if winter and spring were holding hands.

Big gray boulders sat along the slope, covered in thick, soft, emerald moss. Most Ice Orchids grow up in the mossy branches of these old trees, where it's hard to see them. But on the very first boulder, right at the edge of the melting snow, one had settled down low, where Mrs. Claus could see it.
Oh, Kris,
she whispered.

Growing from the moss was a little cluster of tiny bulbs, green blushed with purple, each shaped like a little cone and no bigger than the tip of Mrs. Claus's thumb.
