Their leaves had barely begun to grow. But rising from them, on short stems, were flowers, and they were surprisingly big for such a small plant, each one almost as wide as the palm of Mrs. Claus's hand. Their five narrow, pointed petals were the palest pinkish-purple, spreading out like a star. In the middle was a big white lip, rolled into a tube at the back, with a frilly front edge. The lip was sprinkled with purple and golden-brown spots, as if someone had dotted it with a tiny paintbrush, and right in its center glowed a patch of sunny yellow, lined with rows of tiny soft hairs, like the fuzz on a peach.
It was the Ice Orchid.
Her scientific name is Pleione hookeriana,
said Mrs. Claus softly.

PLEE-oh-nee hook-er-ee-AH-nuh. In an old Greek story, Pleione was the mother of the seven sisters who became the stars called the Pleiades. And hookeriana honors Joseph Dalton Hooker, a British botanist who explored these very mountains about 175 years ago, drawing the plants he found, just like me.
She blooms before her leaf even comes out,
whispered Mrs. Claus, kneeling on a flat rock beside her. The moss was cold and wet under her knees.
Just as the snow melts away. Not a day too early, or the frost would nip her. Not a day too late, or she would miss her pollinator. She waits for exactly the right moment.

Then she did what she always does when she meets a new flower. She didn't hurry. She took out her magnifying glass and looked, slowly and carefully, at every part. She counted the petals. She looked at the frilly edge of the lip, and the tiny spots, and the way the little cone-shaped bulb sat in the moss. She leaned in close and sniffed, and she touched the moss around it, very gently, with one fingertip, to feel how wet it was.

Then she opened her sketchbook and began to draw. First the outline, very lightly, in pencil. Then the details, the ruffles, the spots, the soft hairs on the lip. Then the colors: pale pinkish-purple for the petals, white and sunny yellow for the lip, purple and golden-brown for the spots, green and purple for the bulb, emerald for the moss. At the bottom of the page, she wrote:

Ice Orchid. Growing on a mossy boulder at the edge of melting snow. Flowers before her leaf has grown. Little cone-shaped bulbs, green and purple. Petals pale pinkish-purple. Lip white and frilly, spotted purple and brown, sunny yellow in the center with rows of soft hairs.
Santa waited patiently beside her. He knew that when Mrs. Claus was drawing, she was really seeing, and that was worth waiting for.
Santa was just bending down to look more closely when he heard a soft sound behind them. Fff. Fff. It sounded like a cat sneezing very politely.
Slowly, they turned around.

On a big boulder above them sat a snow leopard. Her fur was thick and soft and smoky gray, almost white, and covered in dark rings and spots, like the patterns of shadows on snow. Her tail was enormous, very long and very fluffy, and she had wrapped it around her paws like a scarf. Her paws were big and round and furry, like a pair of snowshoes. And her eyes were pale and clear, like the mountain sky. Around her edges, her fur shimmered and wavered, the way the air shimmers over a warm stone. She was not an ordinary snow leopard. She was the guardian of the Ice Orchid.
Mrs. Claus felt her heart go thump. But the snow leopard did not growl. She made that gentle sound again, fff, fff, a soft, friendly huffing, the way snow leopards say hello.
You have come for my Ice Orchid,
said the snow leopard. Her voice was low and calm, like wind blowing over snow.
We have,
said Mrs. Claus, bowing her head.
Our reindeer, Blitzen, has lost her balance with the sky. We hope your orchid can teach us how to help her.
Balance,
said the snow leopard, and her long tail swished.
This mountain knows a great deal about balance. Snow and sun. Cold and warmth. Waiting and blooming. My orchid lives right on the line between them.
She stepped down from her boulder, light as a falling snowflake, and sat beside the little pink flowers.
She does not live alone, you know,
the snow leopard went on.

The moss holds the water she drinks. In the moss and the soil live the fungus threads that fed her when she was only a tiny seed. And she needs a visitor, some small flying creature, to carry her pollen from flower to flower, or she can never make seeds of her own. Each one must arrive at just the right time.
Then the snow leopard looked at them with her pale eyes.
Before I share anything with you, tell me something true. What is changing the balance here?
Santa took a deep breath of the thin, cold air. He thought carefully, because he wanted to tell the truth, and to tell it gently.
The world is getting a little warmer,
he said.

So the snow melts at different times than it used to. Sometimes flowers bloom before their bees wake up, or the bees wake up before the flowers are ready. Everything that lives on the edge between winter and spring can feel it.
He paused.
But people all over the world are learning about it, and working to help. And the more we understand, the more we can do.
The snow leopard dipped her head slowly.
That is a true answer,
she said.
And a hopeful one.
Just then, there was a tiny buzzing sound, very faint and very slow. Bzz… bzz…
On the cold rock beside the orchid, a big fuzzy bumblebee was crawling along, very slowly. She tried to lift her wings, but they only trembled.
Oh, the poor thing,
said Mrs. Claus.
She's a queen bumblebee, and she's woken up from her winter sleep, but it's too cold, and she's run out of energy. She's much too tired to fly.

Quickly but gently, Mrs. Claus scooped up a little handful of snow and held it in her warm, cupped hands until it melted into a few clear drops. Then she took off her spectacles and turned them over, so that one round lens made a tiny dish. She tipped the drops into it, added a pinch of sugar from the little tin in her apron pocket, and stirred with her fingertip until the sugar disappeared.
Not honey,
she said softly to Santa.
Honey from other beehives can carry bee sicknesses. Plain sugar and water is safest.
Then she set her spectacles down on the rock, right in front of the bumblebee.

The bee wobbled forward. She stuck out her long, thin tongue and began to drink, sip, sip, sip. Santa and Mrs. Claus held very still and waited. And slowly, slowly, the bee's wings stopped trembling. They began to hum. Bzzz. Then louder. BZZZZZ. And up she rose, circled once around Mrs. Claus's head, as if to say thank you, and zoomed off toward the Ice Orchid. She landed right on one of the pink star-shaped flowers and crawled inside.
Oh, look, she's visiting the orchid!

whispered Mrs. Claus, wiping her spectacles on her apron and popping them back on her nose. She grabbed her pencil and, right beside her drawing of the Ice Orchid, quickly sketched the bumblebee, half inside the pink flower, with her fuzzy bottom sticking out. She wrote beside it:
Queen bumblebee, rescued with sugar water. Visited the Ice Orchid. Was she carrying pollen? Look more closely next time!
The snow leopard's pale eyes shone.
A small kindness,
she said.
But small kindnesses travel far.
Is she the one who carries your orchid's pollen?
asked Santa.
The bumblebee?
The snow leopard tilted her head.
Bumblebees carry pollen for many mountain flowers,
she said.
But who carries my orchid's pollen? That is a secret this mountain is still keeping. Nobody has watched closely enough, for long enough, to know for sure.
Her eyes twinkled.
Perhaps one day a curious child will be the one to find out.
That's how science works,
said Mrs. Claus happily, writing a question mark in her sketchbook.
There's always something still waiting to be discovered.
She bent her head close to the orchid. On the tip of one pale pink petal, a single drop of melted snow was trembling, just about to fall.
Catch it,
said the snow leopard.
Snow that waited for the right moment to melt, on a flower that waited for the right moment to bloom. Take it, and the lesson it carries. Balance. And timing.
Mrs. Claus held a little glass bottle beneath the petal, and the drop slid in with a tiny plink. She corked it and wrote on the label: Ice Orchid. Balance and timing.
Thank you,
she said softly.

Then, just as she had in Lapland, Mrs. Claus opened her aurora lantern. A single drop of northern light floated out and settled on the Ice Orchid's petal like a tiny star. It glowed for a moment, then soaked softly away.
Thank you for teaching us,
she whispered, and the snow leopard's long whiskers twitched, as if she were smiling.
Remember,
said the snow leopard, as she leaped back up onto her boulder.
Magic can help. But the world also needs people who care for it.
And with a last soft fff, she turned, and her shimmering edges blurred into the snow, and she was gone.

By the time Santa and Mrs. Claus made their way back down the zigzag path, the sun was setting, and all the snowy peaks had turned pink and orange and gold, like the tops of giant ice cream cones. In the Sherpa family's warm house, the grandmother had made more dal bhat for dinner, with spicy vegetables on the side. Santa ate three helpings, and then a fourth, and the little boy laughed so hard he nearly fell off his stool.

That night, Mrs. Claus stepped outside before bed. The sky over the Himalayas was so clear and so dark that it was packed with stars, more stars than she had ever seen, thick as spilled sugar, with the misty band of the Milky Way stretching right across the middle. In the field, the four reindeer were sleeping in a cozy heap, and the shaggy yaks were sleeping right beside them, all keeping each other warm.
Mrs. Claus took out her two little glass bottles and held them in her hands.

Then she opened her sketchbook to her drawing of the Ice Orchid, there in the starlight, and this time she knew what to look for. She had drawn the Ice Orchid from the front: five narrow petals spreading out like a star, every one the same distance from the next, all held in perfect balance around the round, frilly cup of her lip. Not too early and not too late, not too much on one side or the other. A star, perfectly balanced.
She unfolded the Winterbreath Verse. There in the margin, beside One stirs the breath of hidden streams, / A pale fire kept in frostbound dreams, was the very same shape.
A pale fire, beside the streams of melting snow,
she whispered.
That's the Ice Orchid. And her rune means Balance.
She drew it carefully at the bottom of her page.
Patience,
she whispered.
And balance.
Santa came out and stood beside her.
Two orchids,
he said.
And three more still waiting for us, each in her own time.

Very early the next morning, Mrs. Claus looked out the window and laughed out loud. The biggest yak was slowly leading the four reindeer up the hillside, hrrrumph, hrrrumph, as if he were giving them a tour. He stopped at a cluster of big gray rocks, and there, growing on the stones, were soft, crinkly patches of pale gray-green lichen. The yak nibbled a little. Comet sniffed it, then Dancer, and then all four reindeer nibbled a little too, crunch, crunch, very happily.
He's showing them the best lichen on the mountain,
said Mrs. Claus.
Yaks eat lichen too, when the grass is thin.
She noticed that the reindeer took only a few bites and left the rest, and she smiled. Lichen grows so slowly that it's always best to leave most of it for next time.

After breakfast, the whole Sherpa family came out to wave goodbye. The little boy gave Vixen a scratch behind the ears, and Vixen nuzzled his hat. The biggest yak said hrrrumph. Then the four reindeer leaped up into the bright blue mountain sky, and the sleigh rose past the prayer flags, flapping their colors in the wind, carrying kind wishes for everyone, everywhere, all the way along the auroral road.
After the Himalayas, the sleigh flew home to the North Pole, because the next orchid wasn't ready to bloom yet. Some things can't be hurried.

Blitzen was waiting in the barn doorway when they landed. Mrs. Claus hugged her neck and showed her the two little glass bottles, and the sketches of the Fairy Slipper and the Ice Orchid, and the bumblebees. Blitzen sniffed each page carefully, as if she were reading them with her nose. Little Lilt wanted to sniff them too, and sneezed, ah-CHOO!, which made everybody laugh.

The summer days at the North Pole were long and bright. The sun circled round and round the sky and never set. The elves played games in the snow at midnight, because it was just as light as noon. And Mrs. Claus checked the scroll every morning.
Then, one day in early summer, the rune beside the painting of the tiny violet lantern began to glow.
Japan,
said Santa, looking at the map.
She's waking up in Japan.

Once again, the elves hurried to pack the sleigh. Once again, Dasher, Dancer, Vixen and Comet lined up in their harnesses, stamping and snorting with excitement. And once again, Santa and Mrs. Claus waved goodbye to Blitzen, and the reindeer leaped onto the auroral road and away.

This time, they flew south and east, across the top of the world. Mrs. Claus peeked over the side of the sleigh. At first, there was only ice below them, a vast white sheet of frozen sea, cracked into giant puzzle pieces with dark blue water in between. Then came land: endless dark forests, rolling hills and wide, winding rivers. And then, at last, the land ended, and there was only sea, deep blue and sparkling and wide, with little white-capped waves far below.
Where is Japan, Kris?
asked Mrs. Claus.
I don't see any land at all.
Keep watching,
said Santa with a twinkle.

And then she saw it. Out in the sparkling blue ocean lay a long, curving line of green islands, like a string of green beads dropped on blue silk. Some were big and some were tiny. The biggest ones were covered from end to end with mountains, all crinkled and folded like a green blanket that someone had pushed together.
That's Japan,
said Santa.
It's a whole country made of islands, thousands of them, in the Pacific Ocean, just off the edge of Asia. Most people live on four big islands. And most of Japan is covered with mountains.

As the sleigh flew closer, Mrs. Claus could see more and more. There were cities along the seashore, with tall buildings that sparkled in the sun. There were tiny farms with flooded rice fields that shone like mirrors, each one reflecting a little square of sky. And there, rising up above the clouds, was a tall, perfect, cone-shaped mountain with snow on its very top, like a scoop of vanilla ice cream on a cone.
Mount Fuji!
gasped Mrs. Claus.

But the rune on the scroll was pointing them farther, into the very heart of the island, where the tallest mountains of Japan stood in a jagged row. Their peaks were still white with snow, even though it was summer down below. The four reindeer swooped down between them, whoosh, into a deep, narrow valley.

It was misty here, and soft gray clouds drifted between the mountaintops like puffs of steam from a teakettle. It was early summer, the rainy season in Japan, and everything was wet and green and dripping. The reindeer landed on a little flat clearing beside a mountain path, their hooves going splosh, splosh, splosh on the soggy ground, and the sleigh slid to a stop.
Santa and Mrs. Claus climbed out and pulled up the hoods of their cloaks. A fine, gentle rain was falling, so soft it was almost like mist. Pitter, patter, pitter.

The path led into a forest of the tallest, straightest trees Mrs. Claus had ever seen: Japanese cedars, with reddish bark that peeled in long strips, and trunks so wide that it would take three people holding hands to reach around them. Their tops disappeared into the mist far above. The air smelled sweet and spicy, of cedar wood and wet earth and rain. Ferns grew everywhere, and thick green moss covered every rock and every root, sparkling with raindrops. Somewhere in the trees, a frog was singing, kero, kero, kero.
Then, from high in a tree, came a chattering sound. Kyaa, kyaa!

Mrs. Claus looked up and nearly dropped her sketchbook. Sitting in the branches was a whole family of monkeys! They had thick, fluffy, silvery-brown fur, short little tails and bright pink-red faces. A mother monkey held a tiny baby against her tummy, and the baby peeked out at Santa with big curious eyes.
Japanese macaques,
whispered Santa.
Some people call them snow monkeys. They live farther north than any other monkey in the world. In winter, when the snow is deep, some of them even warm up in hot springs.

The biggest monkey looked at Santa's red coat and white beard for a long moment, very seriously. Then it scratched its head, as if to say, Well, I've never seen anything like that before, and the whole family scampered off through the branches, rustle, rustle, kyaa!
Mrs. Claus laughed and quickly sketched the baby monkey before she forgot its face.
They walked on, deeper into the mountains. Soon they heard a new sound, faint at first, then louder and louder: a rushing, roaring, splashing sound. Shhhhhhhhh.

The path came out at the edge of a deep, green gorge. High above them, the last snowfields still clung to the peaks, white against the gray sky. And below the snow, the melting water came tumbling down the mountain. It trickled through the moss, seeped from cracks in the rock, gathered into little streams, and finally leaped off a high cliff in a long white waterfall that roared down into a pool far below, sending up clouds of cool, sparkling spray.
This is where the scroll led us,
said Santa, checking the glowing rune.
The little violet lantern doesn't grow in meadows or forests. She grows right on the rock: on wet, mossy cliffs, where melting snow trickles down the stone all spring and summer long.

At the bottom of the stone path, beside a little wooden sign, sat a woman on a folding stool, with a pair of binoculars around her neck and a notebook open on her knees. She wore a green rain jacket and a wide-brimmed hat, and her short gray hair was damp with spray. When she saw them, she stood up, smiled, and gave a small bow.
Good afternoon,
she said.
Have you come to see the Uchōran?

Her name was Dr. Haruko Mori. For many years she had been a botany teacher. Now she was retired, and all through spring and summer she came to this waterfall almost every day as a volunteer, to watch over the little orchids on the cliff.
Watch over them?
asked Santa.
From what?
Dr. Mori sighed.
People love the Uchōran so much that some of them dig her up to take home,
she said.

In many places, the wild ones have become rare. Today, nurseries grow thousands of them in pots, in all sorts of colors, so no one ever needs to take one from the wild. But some people still do. So I sit here, and I count them, and I show visitors how to look without touching.
Mrs. Claus's eyes shone. She opened her sketchbook to show Dr. Mori her drawings, and Dr. Mori opened her notebook to show hers. Both books were full of flowers.
A fellow botanist!
said Dr. Mori, delighted.

Mrs. Claus took a tin of cookies from her basket and gave it to her, and Dr. Mori laughed and gave them two rice balls from her own lunch box: onigiri, neat little triangles of rice wrapped in crisp seaweed.
For the climb,
she said.
You will need your strength.
Then she pointed up the path.
Step only on the flat stones,
she said.
The moss is alive, and her roots are in it. And look closely at where the water runs. That is where she grows.

A narrow path of flat stones climbed up the side of the gorge, slippery with spray. Santa and Mrs. Claus went up it carefully, step by step, holding on to roots and rocks. The closer they came to the waterfall, the louder it roared, SHHHHHHH, until they had to raise their voices to hear each other. Cool, fine spray drifted over their faces like the softest rain, and tiny rainbows sparkled in the mist wherever the sunlight broke through the clouds.
Santa was puzzled.
Linnea,
he called over the roar,
how could a flower possibly grow on a cliff? There's no soil at all. Just rock!
Mrs. Claus stopped and pointed at the cliff beside the waterfall.
Look closely, Kris. Look at how the water moves.

Santa looked. The rock wasn't wet all over. The water came trickling down it in little silver threads, along certain cracks and across certain ledges, the same paths every day, while other parts of the rock stayed dry.
High up the mountain, the snow melts a little at a time,
said Mrs. Claus.

The water runs down the rock along its own special paths, all spring and summer long. Where the water runs, moss grows, and the moss makes a soft, wet little cushion, almost like soil. Our orchid grows right in that moss, exactly where the water trickles. Not too much water, or she'd be washed away. Not too little, or she'd dry out. She has to find just the right spot.
So she reads the cliff,
said Santa slowly,
like a map.
Like a map written in water,
said Mrs. Claus.

They came around a big shoulder of rock and found themselves right beside the waterfall. The cliff next to it glistened, covered in thick, bright green moss, dotted with tiny ferns, and dripping with a hundred silver threads of water. They searched it with their eyes, slowly and carefully, ledge by ledge.
It was Mrs. Claus who saw it first.
There,
she whispered.

On a narrow ledge of moss, just where a thin trickle of meltwater crossed the stone, grew a tiny plant no taller than her hand. It had a few long, narrow leaves, so thin and grassy that you could easily have mistaken them for blades of grass. And from the middle rose a slender stem holding a few small flowers, each one no bigger than a fingertip. They were pinky-purple, like the inside of a seashell, with a wide, three-lobed lip sprinkled with darker purple spots, as if someone had flicked a paintbrush at them. Behind each flower curved a thin little tube, called a spur. In the misty light by the waterfall, the little flowers seemed to glow, like tiny lanterns.
It was the Frost Lantern.
Ponerorchis graminifolia,
breathed Mrs. Claus.

po-ner-OR-kis gram-ih-nih-FO-lee-uh. Graminifolia means 'grass-leaved,' because her leaves look just like blades of grass. In Japan she is called Uchōran, oo-CHOH-ran, and people here have loved her for a very long time. Some scientists now call her Hemipilia graminifolia. Names can change as scientists learn more about how plants are related.
She's growing exactly where the water runs,
said Mrs. Claus, full of wonder.
A hand's width to the left, and the rock would dry out by midsummer. A hand's width to the right, and the waterfall would wash her away.

She found a dry rock to sit on and got out her magnifying glass and sketchbook. She looked at the narrow leaves, the spots on the lip, the curving spurs, and the way the whole little plant leaned toward the trickling water as if it were listening to it. Then she began to draw, carefully and slowly, while Santa held his cloak over her to keep the spray off her paper. Underneath, she wrote:
Frost Lantern. Growing in wet moss on a cliff beside a waterfall, exactly where the snowmelt trickles. Grass-like leaves. A few small pink-purple flowers, spotted lip, long spur.
Just as she finished, a tiny bee, no bigger than her thumbnail, zigzagged through the cool air beside the falls. It hovered over the Frost Lantern and then landed on one of the little flowers.
Mrs. Claus quickly drew it in the corner of her page. Then she tapped her pencil against her chin.
I wonder,
she said.
Is that little bee carrying her pollen? Nobody knows for sure who the Frost Lantern's pollinator is. Scientists haven't watched her closely enough yet to find out.
She wrote beside the bee: Small bee, visiting. Pollinator? Nobody knows yet!
A mystery,
said Santa, delighted.
The best kind,
said Mrs. Claus.
The kind still waiting for someone to solve it.
Then the wind changed.

A cool breeze swirled around them, curling and twisting in a way that ordinary wind never does. It caught the spray from the waterfall and spun it into a tall, shimmering, misty shape. The shape grew taller and clearer until a figure stood on the wet rock in front of them. It was tall and slender, made of swirling air and fine sparkling mist, with long hair that streamed out behind it like blowing spray, and eyes the pale blue of distant ice. When it moved, it made a soft sound, whooo, like wind blowing through a tunnel. Its feet didn't leave any footprints at all. The water droplets on the moss simply rearranged themselves a little wherever it stepped.
Mrs. Claus wasn't frightened. It felt like meeting the wind itself, polite and curious.
I am the Wind-Guide,
said the figure, in a voice like air slipping between stones.
I know every path the wind and water take through these mountains. You have come for my Frost Lantern.
We have,
said Mrs. Claus.
Our reindeer Blitzen has lost her way with the sky. We're hoping your orchid can help us understand.
The Wind-Guide tilted its misty head.
Then answer me this,
it said.
What is the difference between being lost, and not yet knowing the way?
Mrs. Claus looked at the little orchid, leaning toward the trickling water. She thought for a long time.
If you're lost,
she said slowly,

it means you've forgotten where you belong. But this orchid isn't lost. She knows exactly where to grow, because she pays attention. To the slope, to the water, to the way it trickles down the rock. She listens to the mountain.
Santa nodded.
And Blitzen isn't lost either,
he said.
She's still home in her barn, with all of us who love her. She has just forgotten how to listen to the sky. And listening can be learned again.
The Wind-Guide's misty face softened into something like a smile.
Yes,
it said.

Not knowing the way is not the same as being lost. It is an invitation to slow down, and listen, and pay closer attention. The way is always there, written in the world, for anyone who is willing to read it.

Then it knelt, with a little swirl of air, and breathed out softly over the falls. A wisp of silvery mist drifted up from the spray, curling like a tiny cloud, and inside it, very faintly, you could still hear the sound of the falling water.
Mist that remembers the song of the water,
said the Wind-Guide.
Take it, and take my lesson with it.

Mrs. Claus held out a little glass bottle, and the Wind-Guide guided the wisp inside as gently as a snowflake. When she held the bottle up to her ear, she could still hear the waterfall, very far away. On the label she wrote: Frost Lantern. Listen.
What can we give you in return?
she asked.
The Wind-Guide thought for a moment.
Tell the children about her,
it said.
Tell them she is small and easy to miss, and that some people have taken her from the wild because she is so beautiful. Tell them to leave her on her cliff, where the water sings to her.
We promise,
said Mrs. Claus.

Then Mrs. Claus opened her aurora lantern, and a single drop of northern light floated out. It settled on the little violet flower, glowing like a tiny star above the trickling water, then soaked softly away.
Thank you for teaching us,
she whispered.
Then, with a last swirl of mist, whooo, the Wind-Guide drifted back into the spray of the waterfall, and was gone.

As they climbed back down the slippery stones, Mrs. Claus looked at her drawing again: the tiny flower's little hood, her lip spreading out below in three parts, and, behind the hood, her thin spur curling around like a little ear. And suddenly she stopped.
Kris,
she said.
Look.

The hood, the spreading lip and the curling spur made a shape. She unfolded the Winterbreath Verse, and there in the margin, beside One wakes the glow where shadows lie, / A lantern made of lullaby, was the very same rune.
A lantern,
she whispered,
that glows in the shadows by the waterfall, and sings like a lullaby. That's the Frost Lantern.
She looked at the little spur, curled like an ear, as if the flower were listening to the falls.
And her rune means Listen.
She drew it at the bottom of her page. On the scroll, the rune beside the little violet lantern stopped flickering and shone steady and silver.

As they walked back through the cedar forest, the rain stopped, and the clouds began to part. High above them, a big brown bird called a black kite circled lazily on the warm air, and from somewhere far down the valley came the slow, deep bonnnng of a temple bell.
At the bottom of the stone path, Dr. Mori was still on her folding stool, counting. Mrs. Claus told her all about the tiny bee.
A pollinator nobody knows yet?
said Dr. Mori, and she wrote it carefully in her notebook. Then she smiled.
Then someone will have to find out.
The four reindeer were waiting in the clearing, their antlers dripping with rain. Dasher stamped a happy hoof when she saw them, as if to say, What took you so long?
Three orchids,
said Mrs. Claus, as the sleigh rose up over the misty mountains, past the snowy peak of Mount Fuji and out over the sparkling sea.
Three runes. Wait. Balance. Listen.
And two more to go,
said Santa.
Far away at the North Pole, Blitzen lifted her head in the barn. For just a moment, she thought she heard something, very faint, like a song she used to know, drifting down from the sky.
Not long after they came home from Japan, the rune beside the painting of the ghost-white bells began to glow.
North America,
said Santa, tracing the silver dotted line across the map with his finger.
A mountain in the Pacific Northwest.
Mrs. Claus leaned over his shoulder, and her eyes went soft.
A white orchid,
she said quietly.
Blooming beside the snow on a great mountain.

So once more, the elves packed the sleigh. Once more, Dasher, Dancer, Vixen and Comet stamped and snorted in their harnesses. And once more, Blitzen came to the barn door to see them off. This time, she stepped right up to the sleigh and pressed her warm nose against Mrs. Claus's cheek, for a long, long moment, before she stepped back.
Up onto the auroral road they leaped, and away.

This time, they flew south across the frozen Arctic Ocean, and then over a wide, flat land of moss and little lakes that sparkled like broken mirrors. It was the tundra of Alaska, where no trees grow, because the ground deep down stays frozen all year round.
Kris, look!
cried Mrs. Claus.

Far below, a great river of brown animals was moving across the tundra. There were hundreds and hundreds of them, maybe thousands, walking together in long, winding lines, with antlers bobbing like a forest on the move.
Caribou,
said Santa, smiling.

Our reindeer's cousins! Caribou and reindeer are really the very same animal, with two different names. These ones are wild, and every year they walk hundreds and hundreds of miles across the tundra, all together.
Comet tossed her antlers and gave a happy snort, as if waving hello to her cousins.

Then the sleigh followed the coast, south and south and south. They flew over snowy mountains that came right down to the sea, where giant rivers of ice, called glaciers, crept down the valleys and broke off at the water's edge in great blue-white chunks, KER-SPLASH!, into the ocean. They flew over hundreds of green, forested islands, scattered in the sea like stepping stones. And down in the dark blue water, Mrs. Claus spotted a puff of mist, then another, and then a huge dark back curving up out of the waves, and a giant tail lifting high in the air before it slipped back down, sploosh.
A whale!
she gasped.
A humpback whale!

At last they came to a land of deep green forests and silver-blue water, with mountains rising behind it. And standing up above all the other mountains, all by itself, so enormous that it seemed to have its own weather, was one gigantic mountain, white from top to bottom with snow and ice, shining in the sun like a giant scoop of vanilla ice cream.
That's Mount Rainier,
said Santa softly.

The tallest mountain in Washington State. But it had names long before that one. The Native peoples who live all around it have many names for it, in many languages. Some of those names mean 'the white mountain,' and some speak of the mountain as a mother, whose snow gives water and food to everything below.

As the sleigh circled closer, Mrs. Claus could see that the mountain was striped with glaciers, cracked and blue, like frosting on a giant cake. Lower down, there were wide meadows, where patches of snow were melting, and the ground beside them was splashed with purple and red and yellow wildflowers. And lower still, wrapped all around the mountain like a thick green scarf, was an ancient forest.
The rune on the scroll glowed brighter.
In the forest,
said Santa.
Down where the shade is deep.
The four reindeer glided down and landed in a little clearing beside the forest, thump, thump, thump, thump, and the sleigh slid to a stop on a cushion of moss and fallen needles.
Santa and Mrs. Claus climbed out, and they both stood very still. It was the quietest forest they had ever been in.

The trees were giants. Douglas firs and red cedars and hemlocks, so tall that their tops were lost somewhere far, far above, and so wide at the bottom that you could have parked the whole sleigh behind just one of them. Their trunks were furry with green moss. Long, pale green strands of lichen hung from the branches like old men's beards. The sunlight came down through the leaves in little gold coins and sprinkled across the forest floor. And the floor itself was soft and springy, covered in moss, ferns and fallen logs, with tiny new trees growing right out of the old logs, like children sitting on their grandparents' laps.

The air was cool and damp and smelled of wet bark, cedar, mushrooms and rich, dark earth. The only sounds were a stream gurgling somewhere nearby and, far off in the trees, the strange, dreamy whistle of a bird, one long, quivering note, wheeeeee, then quiet, then another note, a little higher.
That's a varied thrush,
said Mrs. Claus.
He always sounds like he's whistling through a little tin can.
In the shadiest places, under the biggest trees, there were still patches of old snow, gray-white and slowly melting. Even though it was summer, the snow lasted longer here, hidden from the sun.
They started down a narrow path, walking softly. Santa stopped suddenly and pointed at the ground.
Linnea! What on earth is that?
Creeping slowly across the path was a big, fat, bright yellow slug, as long as Santa's hand, with little black spots and two pairs of wiggly feelers on its head.
Mrs. Claus laughed.
That's a banana slug! They live in these forests. They're nature's clean-up crew. They eat fallen leaves and old mushrooms and turn them back into soil.
Santa very carefully stepped over the banana slug, and the banana slug very slowly carried on its way.
As they walked, Santa kept looking around, puzzled.
Linnea,
he said at last,
how can any flower grow down here? It's so shady. Plants need sunshine to make their food, don't they? That's why their leaves are green.
Most plants do,
said Mrs. Claus, and her eyes twinkled behind her spectacles, because she loved this question.

Their green leaves catch sunlight and turn it into sugar, which is their food. But the orchid we're looking for is different. She has no green leaves at all. Not a single speck of green. She can't make her own food from sunlight.
Santa's bushy eyebrows went up.
Then how does she eat?
Mrs. Claus knelt down and tapped the mossy ground.

Under our feet, there's a hidden forest, Kris. It's made of fungus threads, finer than hairs, and there are miles and miles of them, wrapped around the roots of all these big trees. The trees make sugar up in their needles, high in the sunshine, and they share some of it with the fungus. The fungus brings the trees water and minerals from the soil. They trade with each other, all day long.
Like a market,
said Santa slowly.
Under the ground.
Exactly like a market,
said Mrs. Claus.

And our orchid taps right into it. She takes a tiny bit of sugar from the fungus, which got it from the trees. So really, she's fed by the whole forest, all working together. If the old trees were cut down, or the fungus threads were broken, she couldn't live here anymore.
Santa looked around at the giant trees with new eyes.
So the whole forest is holding hands,
he said,
underground, where nobody can see.
Yes,
said Mrs. Claus softly.
That's a lovely way to say it.

They searched for a long time, slowly and patiently, peeking under ferns and around logs and behind the great roots of the cedars. They passed the last patches of melting snow, drip, drip. And then, at the foot of an enormous red cedar, right beside a little snowbank that was melting into the moss, Mrs. Claus stopped and caught her breath.
Kris,
she whispered.
Don't move.

Rising from the dark soil, right at the edge of the snow, stood a little cluster of flowers so white that they almost seemed to glow, like candles in the shade. Their stems were white. Their flowers were white. There was not a single speck of green anywhere, only white, as pale and smooth as porcelain, with just a tiny touch of golden yellow deep inside each blossom. Each stem held several flowers, like little hooded bells, and they all leaned close together, as if sharing a secret.
It was the Phantom Orchid.
Her scientific name is Cephalanthera austiniae,
whispered Mrs. Claus.

sef-uh-LAN-thur-uh AW-stin-ee-ee. Cephalanthera means 'head-anther,' for the little cap of pollen at the very tip of her column. And austiniae honors Rebecca Austin, a botanist in California more than a hundred years ago, who collected wild plants and sent them to scientists so they could be studied.
They look like ghosts, Santa thought. But not frightening ones. More like snowflakes that had decided to become flowers.

Mrs. Claus knelt very carefully, so she wouldn't disturb the soil, and took out her magnifying glass. She looked for a long time. She counted the flowers on each stem. She looked at the little yellow patch inside. She noticed that the stems looked waxy, almost like candles, and that the cluster grew right where the snow was melting into the moss. Then she opened her sketchbook and drew, slowly and carefully. When she had finished the flowers, she added something else: very faint, fine lines spreading out through the soil beneath them, for the fungus threads that no one could see. Then she wrote:
Phantom Orchid. Mount Rainier. Blooming beside a melting snowbank at the foot of a giant cedar. All white, no green at all. Fed by the forest through the fungus threads.
Just then, they heard voices coming along the trail. Laughing, chattering voices, and footsteps.
Quick as a wink, Santa and Mrs. Claus stepped behind the great cedar trunk.

Around the bend came a group of teenagers with backpacks and hiking boots, out exploring the mountain together. Most of them walked right past. But one girl stopped. She had spotted the little white flowers glowing beside the snow. She knelt down, very slowly and very gently, and looked at them for a long, long time, her eyes wide with wonder. She didn't pick them. She just looked.
Come on!
called her friends from up the trail.
Coming!
she called back. But before she stood up, she whispered to the flowers,
I'm going to remember you forever.
Then she ran to catch up with her friends.
Behind the cedar, Mrs. Claus pressed her hand to her heart.
Someday,
she whispered to Santa,
she'll tell her children about the white orchid she saw blooming in the snow. And maybe one of them will grow up to love orchids too.
Santa smiled.
Some seeds are planted in people,
he said.

They stepped back out beside the orchids. And this time, it was Santa who noticed something moving. A tiny bee, much smaller than a bumblebee, slim and shiny and dark, was crawling into one of the white bells.
Linnea, look, a visitor!
Mrs. Claus quickly drew the little bee beside her orchid, with its shiny dark body and see-through wings, and wrote: A small sweat bee, visiting the Phantom Orchid. Then she smiled.
Scientists have seen little sweat bees just like this one carrying her pollen,
she said.
And if no bee comes, she can even pollinate herself. But even a ghost flower is glad to have a friend.

As she finished her drawing, the forest grew very quiet. The moss beneath their knees gave a little shiver, though there was no wind. And slowly, from the soil in front of the orchids, something began to rise.

It didn't burst up. It came into view gently, the way your eyes slowly notice shapes in the dark. It was tall and graceful, and its whole body was woven from countless fine white threads, like the fungus threads under the ground, all twisting and branching together. Where its face should be, the threads made a soft, shifting pattern, like frost on a window. It glowed faintly, as gentle as moonlight.
Mrs. Claus wasn't afraid. She felt as if she were meeting someone who had been there all along, quietly holding everything together.
Welcome, seekers,
said the Mycelial Spirit, the guardian of the Phantom Orchid. Its voice seemed to come from everywhere at once: from the roots, the soil, the ferns, the moss. It was low and soft and kind.
You have found the one who lives entirely on the kindness of others.
Santa bowed his head.
We've come to learn from her,
he said.
Not to take her away.
Good,
said the spirit.
She could never live in a pot on a windowsill. She belongs here, with the trees and the threads and the snow.
Some things we can only love by letting them stay where they belong,
said Mrs. Claus softly.
The white threads of the spirit glowed a little brighter, as if it were smiling.
You are worried about your reindeer,
said the spirit.
Blitzen,
said Santa.
She's lost her feeling for the sky. And we've seen so many other things changing too. Sometimes it's hard not to worry.
The spirit turned toward the white orchids.
Look at her,
it said.

She cannot feed herself. All alone, she could never live. And yet, here she is, blooming. Because she is held up by the whole forest: the trees, the fungus, the rain, the snow, even the little bee. She isn't strong because she does everything by herself. She is strong because she is connected.
Like Blitzen,
Mrs. Claus whispered.
Blitzen doesn't fly by herself either. She has her herd, and us, and the elves who love her, and the children who believe in her.
Just so,
said the spirit.
When she remembers that, she will remember how to fly. Nobody flies alone. Nobody blooms alone. Nobody heals alone.

Then the spirit touched one threaded finger to the soil beside the orchids, away from their roots, and drew it slowly upward. A single thread of soft white light rose out of the ground, glowing like a strand of moonlight: a tiny piece of the forest's hidden web.
A thread of the web that holds us all together,
said the spirit.
It takes nothing from the forest, because the web is made of sharing. Take it, and take the lesson with it.
Mrs. Claus held out a little glass bottle, and the glowing thread coiled gently inside, like a sleeping firefly. She corked it and wrote on the label: Phantom Orchid. We never fly alone.

In return, Mrs. Claus opened her aurora lantern. A single drop of northern light floated down and settled on the tallest white stem, so that for a moment the Phantom Orchid glowed like a real lantern in the shade. Then the light soaked softly away.
Thank you for teaching us,
she whispered. And all around them, the white threads in the soil seemed to shimmer, just for a moment.
Thank you,
said Santa to the spirit.
Remember,
said the spirit, as it began to sink gently back into the soil, its threads untangling and fading into the moss,
even when you can't see them, the threads are there.
And then it was gone, and only the white orchids remained, glowing softly beside the melting snow, as if nothing unusual had happened at all.

As the sleigh rose up out of the forest, the sun was setting, and the snowy top of Mount Rainier turned pink, then rosy orange, then glowing gold, like a giant lantern in the sky. Mrs. Claus looked down over the side of the sleigh. And for just one heartbeat, she thought she saw something impossible: faint, glowing threads beneath the forest, stretching from tree to tree to orchid to stream, and then on and on, north and north, all the way toward a red barn far away, under the summer sun, where a reindeer was waiting.
Then the colors of the auroral road folded around them, and it was gone.
Far away in the barn, Blitzen lifted her head from the straw, as if she had heard someone whisper, You are not alone.

Mrs. Claus opened her sketchbook on her lap and looked at her drawing of the Phantom Orchid: one white stem, and all along it, the little white flowers, every one held on the very same stem, like bells on a single string. And underneath, the fine lines she had drawn for the fungus threads, joining that stem to the trees, to the stream, to everything.

She already knew. She unfolded the Winterbreath Verse, and there in the margin, beside One guards the roots where forest sleeps, / Its petals warm the dark it keeps, was the very same shape: a single stem, with flowers held all along it.
Every flower held on one stem,
whispered Mrs. Claus,
and the stem held by the whole forest. She's connected to everything around her. Her rune means Belong.
She drew it at the bottom of her page. Then she counted the runes on her pages.
Wait. Balance. Listen. Belong.
She looked up at Santa.
We are all part of something bigger, Kris. The trees, the fungus, the bees, the girl on the trail, Blitzen, us. All of it is connected.
Four orchids,
said Santa.
And one more still to find.

This time, they did not go home first. By the time the sleigh rose away from Mount Rainier, the last rune on the scroll, the one beside the painting of the silver-veined leaf, had already begun to glow.
East,
said Santa, studying the map.
To the Rocky Mountains.

The four reindeer turned, and the sleigh flew east, over the snowy tops of the Cascade Mountains, where more sleeping volcanoes stood in a row like giant white cones. On the other side, the land changed completely. The wet green forests were gone. Below them now stretched wide, dry hills the color of a lion's fur, and huge golden fields of wheat that rippled in the wind. A great river wound through them, deep blue and shining, carving its way between tall brown cliffs.
Then, ahead of them, rising up from the earth like the back of a sleeping giant, came the mountains.
The Rocky Mountains,
said Santa.
They're one of the longest chains of mountains in the world. They run all the way down the middle of North America, from northern Canada almost to Mexico, thousands of miles long.

The Rockies were jagged and gray, with snow still tucked into their highest hollows, even now at the end of summer. Mrs. Claus spotted a family of mountain goats clinging to a cliff so steep it looked impossible, shaggy and white as snowballs, with little black horns. Far below, in a sunny clearing, a mother black bear and her cub were eating berries from the bushes, paying no attention at all to the sleigh passing high above.

The rune led them to a deep, hidden valley in the northern Rockies, where a cold, clear creek ran between the mountains. Along the creek grew an ancient forest of giant red cedars and hemlocks, so old and so tall and so green that it felt like stepping back in time.
A rainforest,
said Mrs. Claus, amazed,
right here in the middle of the mountains, far from the sea. The snow that melts off these peaks every summer keeps it wet all year long.
The four reindeer glided down and landed beside the creek, thump, thump, thump, thump, on a bank of soft moss. Dasher went straight to the creek and took a long, cold drink, slurp, slurp.

Santa and Mrs. Claus walked into the forest. It was cool and shady and very quiet. The cedar trunks were broad as barn doors, their reddish bark twisting slowly upward in long ridges, like the stripes on a candy cane. Ferns grew waist-high. In the deepest shade, at the foot of a north-facing cliff, one last patch of old snow still lay melting, gray and crusty, drip, drip. The air smelled of cedar, wet moss, and something sweet and fruity.
Huckleberries!
said Santa, spotting a bush covered in tiny dark purple berries. He picked one and popped it in his mouth. It was sweet and tart at the same time, like a blueberry that had learned to sing.
Oh, my,
he said, and picked a few more, and gave half to Mrs. Claus.
Somewhere in the ferns, a tiny brown bird sang a song that seemed far too big for it, a long, bubbling, tumbling cascade of notes that went on and on.
A wren,
said Mrs. Claus, smiling.
The smallest bird in the forest, with the biggest song.
They walked slowly between the cedars, looking low, the way Mrs. Claus had taught Santa to look. And this time, it was Santa who stopped first.
Linnea,
he said.
Is that her?

At the foot of the biggest cedar of all, near the edge of the melting snow, lay a little cluster of leaves pressed flat against the moss in a rosette, like the petals of a green rose. Each leaf was dark green, glossy and cool, no longer than Mrs. Claus's thumb. Down the middle of every leaf ran a bright white stripe. And on these particular plants, the white didn't stop there: a web of fine silver-white veins spread out from the stripe across the whole leaf, crossing and branching like the scales on a snake's back, or the lines between the pieces of a stained-glass window.

And rising from the middle of the rosette was a slender flower stalk, about as tall as Mrs. Claus's hand, wound round and round with tiny white flowers, each no bigger than a grain of rice, climbing up the stem in a soft spiral, like a spiral staircase.
It was the Rattlesnake Plantain.
Mrs. Claus knelt down so fast that her knees sank into the moss.
Oh, there you are,
she breathed.
Goodyera oblongifolia,
said Mrs. Claus happily.

GOOD-yer-uh ob-long-ih-FO-lee-uh. Goodyera is named for John Goodyer, an English plant-lover who lived about four hundred years ago. And oblongifolia simply means 'with oblong leaves.' Scientists often name plants after people, or after the way they look.
Rattlesnake?
said Santa.
That's an odd name for something so pretty.
Mrs. Claus laughed.
It's the leaves. People thought the pattern looked like snakeskin, and long ago some believed the plant could cure snakebites. It can't, but the name stuck.

She brushed aside a few fallen needles, and her eyes widened. Beside the first rosette was another, and another, and another. A whole little village of them, spread in a curve around the cedar's roots.
They're connected underground,
she whispered.

She sends out creeping stems under the moss, and new rosettes sprout along them. Each rosette blooms once, and then makes way for new ones, but the family keeps on growing, a little farther every year. This colony might be older than both of us put together.
Beside the blooming stalk stood another one, dry and brown and papery: last year's flower stalk, still standing, with split-open seed pods along it.

Just then, a big, round bumblebee came humming through the ferns, bzzzzzz. She landed at the very bottom of the flower spike and began to climb, flower by flower, round and round, up the spiral staircase, sipping a tiny drop of sweet nectar from each one.
Look, Kris!
whispered Mrs. Claus.
Bumblebees usually start at the bottom and climb up. And this little orchid really does have nectar for her, a real treat, not a trick.

She got out her magnifying glass and her sketchbook, and she drew for a long, happy time: the rosette, then one leaf, tracing the silver veins line by line, then the spiral of tiny white flowers, and the bumblebee halfway up, with her fuzzy legs hugging the stem. Underneath, she wrote:

Rattlesnake Plantain. A colony of rosettes at the foot of an old cedar, connected underground. Dark green leaves netted with silver veins. Tiny white flowers spiraling up the stem. Visited by a bumblebee, climbing bottom to top, drinking nectar.
Every leaf is different,
she murmured, looking closely.
The pattern is never quite the same twice. But it's always the same kind of pattern.
Then the old cedar beside them gave a long, low creak, like a ship easing at anchor. Flakes of bark and lichen drifted down onto the moss.
And the cedar began to move.

It didn't split or break. One of the long twisting ridges of bark simply stepped forward and became a shoulder. Another became an arm. And slowly, a face settled out of the furrowed wood: old beyond counting, grooved and gentle, with eyes the deep, quiet green of a forest at dusk. Its hair was a curtain of feathery cedar branches. Moss grew on its shoulders, along with a few tiny mushrooms and one curious little brown wren, who didn't seem bothered in the least.
The Elder of the Forest,
said Santa softly, and he bowed his head low. Mrs. Claus closed her sketchbook and bowed too.
When the Elder spoke, its voice was slow and deep, like the wind moving through a whole valley of trees at once.
Welcome, Claus. And Linnea, who draws what she does not take.
Its green eyes turned to the little rosettes.
You have found my oldest neighbor.
Your neighbor?
asked Mrs. Claus.
She was growing at my roots before your grandmother's grandmother was born,
said the Elder. It bent down until its great bark face was close to the ground.
You have come a long way. I can smell it on you: Lapland spruce and Himalayan stone, waterfall spray and the deep forest of the great mountain. Four orchids. Four lessons.
We've come for the fifth,
said Santa.
For Blitzen.
Then tell me,
said the Elder.
The other orchids you visited rest through the winter. They drop their leaves, or sleep underground. But this one does not. What does she do when winter comes?
Santa looked at Mrs. Claus, and Mrs. Claus's eyes twinkled.
She stays green,
said Mrs. Claus.

All winter long, her leaves stay right here, under the snow. The snow is like a thick, fluffy blanket. Under it, the ground hardly freezes, so her leaves stay safe. And on bright days, when a little light shines through the snow, she can even keep making a little food.
That is how she does it,
said the Elder.
But why?
Mrs. Claus was quiet for a long moment, looking at the silver-veined leaves.
Because she isn't trying to bloom in winter,
she said at last.
She's just staying alive, keeping a little green going, so that when summer comes back, she doesn't have to start over from nothing. She's ready.
She smiled.
She doesn't need to be beautiful in the middle of winter. She only needs to still be here.
The Elder's eyes crinkled at the corners, and a few cedar needles drifted down from its branches.
Yes,
it said.

Many think strength is the big leap, the bright bloom, the flight. But much of strength is quieter than that. It is staying green. It is keeping hope alive through the long, dark, cold months, so that when the light comes back, you are ready.
Then the Elder breathed out, a long, slow breath that smelled of cedar and rain.

And for one magical moment, summer disappeared. The air turned icy. Deep, soft snow lay all around them, glowing blue in the dim winter light, and the forest was silent. There was no flower spike, no bumblebee, no huckleberries. But under the snow, where the Elder had brushed a little window clear, the dark green leaves were still there, alive and green, their silver veins shining, quietly waiting. Beside them stood one tall, dry, old flower stalk, straight up out of the snow.
Then the Elder breathed in, and it was summer again.

Mrs. Claus quickly opened her sketchbook and drew what she had seen in the vision, before she could forget it: one tall, straight old flower stalk standing up through the winter snow, with last year's seed pods still winding round and round it in a spiral, all the way to the top, and the green leaves waiting below.
And then she gasped.
Kris. It's the last rune!

She unfolded the Winterbreath Verse. In the margin, beside One hums where ancient winds arise, / A song that threads through frozen skies, was the very same shape: a straight stem standing through the winter, with a spiral winding up around it.
Threads through frozen skies,
she whispered, looking at the spiral climbing the old stalk.
Even in the middle of winter, she is still reaching up, still holding on to her seeds. Her rune means Hope.
She drew it at the bottom of her page. On the scroll, the last rune stopped flickering and shone steady and silver.
Now look closer,
said the Elder gently.
Look at the leaf.

They bent over the rosette. The silver veins crossed and recrossed in the dark green, branching, joining and curving back. Mrs. Claus held her sketchbook up beside it, with all five of her new runes drawn at the bottoms of the pages. Then she held up the scroll, with its runes around the border. And she caught her breath.
Every single rune, the five new ones, and the old ones on the scroll, and the ones on Firstlight's antlers, was drawn on the very same crisscross of lines. The veins of this leaf.
The Reindeer Runes,
she whispered.
They were written in the pattern of this leaf, all along. This little leaf is the key to all of them.
Mrs. Claus laughed with delight.
Oh, Snowbell will be so happy,
she said.
The library elves have a song about these runes, you know. Snowbell taught it to us while we were packing.
Santa chuckled.
And I remember every word,
he said. And there in the green cedar valley, with the leaf in Mrs. Claus's hand and the runes glowing softly on the scroll, Santa sang it in his deep, rumbling voice.
When the song ended, the Elder's great branches swayed slowly, and a few cedar needles sifted down from them like sugar.
The elves sing it more sweetly than the old ones did,
it said, in its deep, creaking voice.
But the words are the same. I have watched those runes grow on these leaves for a thousand winters.
Mrs. Claus smiled, and the last notes of the song seemed to hang in the cool, still air of the cedar wood like the ringing of a little bell.
Then Mrs. Claus remembered something, and her heart began to beat a little faster.
Firstlight's antlers,
she said.
The three runes Snowbell could read. Winter. Root. Flight.
She looked down at the little colony of rosettes, all joined together under the moss by their creeping stems.
Root. Flight that grows from a root.
You are close,
said the Elder.
But the rest of Firstlight's message was never meant to be read on old antlers. It will be written on new ones, when the time is right.
New antlers,
whispered Mrs. Claus. She thought of Blitzen, far away in the barn, and her new antlers growing all summer under their soft brown velvet.
You wish to carry something home,
said the Elder.
Only what she can spare,
said Mrs. Claus.
Nothing living.

The Elder nodded. With great care, it reached to the edge of the colony and picked up a single old leaf that had already come loose from its rosette, faded at the edges but with its silver pattern still clear.
This leaf has finished its work,
it said.
Four winters it stayed green. Now it is ready to become soil. Let it carry the lesson for you.
Mrs. Claus held out a paper envelope, and the Elder laid the leaf inside. She wrote on the front: Rattlesnake Plantain. Hope.

Then she opened her aurora lantern one last time on this journey. A single drop of northern light floated down and settled on a silver-veined leaf, glowing like a tiny star in the cedar shade. It shimmered, then soaked softly away.
Thank you for teaching us,
she whispered. The wren on the Elder's shoulder sang its enormous song, as if to say, You're welcome.
The Elder rose to its full height, until its feathery branches brushed the lower limbs of the trees. Already it was settling back into the trunk, ridge by ridge.
Take this to your reindeer,
it said.

Tell her that some seasons are for leaping, and some are for staying green. Both are part of flight. And tell her that everything she has ever given, every night she carried the sleigh, every child who looked up and saw her, comes back to her, again and again, like the veins of a leaf that always return to the stem.
And then it was only a cedar again: old and vast, its bark twisting slowly toward the sky, with a wren at its feet.
For a long while, neither of them spoke.

Then Mrs. Claus opened her satchel and laid all five of her treasures side by side on her knees: four little glass bottles and one paper envelope. She opened her sketchbook and turned the pages, one by one, to the five runes she had drawn.
Wait,
she said, touching the first.
Balance. Listen. Belong.
She touched the last.
Hope.
Five orchids,
said Santa softly.
Five lessons,
said Mrs. Claus.
And I think they all belong together, like the threads of a leaf.
Santa helped her up, and together they walked back between the great cedars, past the huckleberry bushes, to where the four reindeer waited by the creek, their antlers glowing faintly silver.
Home,
said Santa, taking up the reins.

Far to the north, in the barn, Blitzen was resting in the straw. Her new antlers had grown tall and branched all summer long, and now, at the very end of summer, the soft brown velvet that covered them was beginning to loosen and peel, the way it always does for reindeer when their new antlers are finished growing. Underneath, the new antlers were smooth and pale and clean, and completely blank.
For a little while now, Blitzen had stopped trying so hard to fly. She was simply resting: warm, and still, and waiting. And for the first time in a long time, it didn't feel like failing.
It felt like staying green.
Five little treasures sat in a row on the kitchen windowsill: four glass bottles and one paper envelope. Every night, Mrs. Claus looked at them. And every morning, she walked out to the barn.

Blitzen's new antlers were tall and smooth now. The soft brown velvet was gone. But when the other reindeer practiced over the barn roof, her hooves still made no sound at all. No click. No tingle. Nothing.
Five orchids,
Mrs. Claus said quietly, stroking Blitzen's neck.
Five lessons. And still something is missing.
That evening, she unrolled the old scroll on the kitchen table, the way she had done a hundred times before. Santa leaned over her shoulder with his mug of cocoa.
Kris,
she whispered.
Look at the bottom.

At the very bottom of the scroll, below the five paintings, where the paper had gone brown and soft with age, something was glowing. They had always thought it was just an old stain, left by melting snow. But now, little by little, a sixth painting was coming back into the light: a tiny white flower, no bigger than a thumbnail, growing in a marsh of round green cushions, beneath a mountain covered in ice.
Beside it, a single rune glowed silver-blue.
Six,
breathed Santa.
There were six all along.
He traced the silver dotted line on the map with his finger. Down, down, down it went, past the middle of the world, all the way to the long spine of mountains on the western side of South America.
The Andes,
said Mrs. Claus.
Peru.
And look how high,
said Santa, tapping the map.
Higher than the Himalayan village. Higher than almost anywhere a flower can grow.

This time, Blitzen came out to the sleigh to see them off. She pressed her nose against the old scroll, very gently, as if she could smell the snow on that faraway mountain. Then she lifted her head and looked at Mrs. Claus with her deep blue eyes.
We'll find it,
Mrs. Claus promised.
The last one.
Dasher, Dancer, Vixen and Comet leaped onto the auroral road, and the sleigh swept south.

They flew over the frozen Arctic Ocean and the dark green forests of Canada, over prairies and deserts and the bright blue water of the Caribbean Sea. They crossed the middle of the world, where the sun shines straight down, and flew on over the endless green of the Amazon rainforest, where great brown rivers twisted like ribbons and steam rose from the trees.
Then, ahead of them, a wall of mountains rose out of the green. The peaks were sharp and gray and frosted white at the very top, and glaciers hung on their shoulders like great blue-white scarves.
The Andes,
said Santa softly.
The longest mountains in the world.

The sleigh dipped down through a cloud, wet and cold, and came out into sunshine so bright that Mrs. Claus had to shade her eyes. Below them, a deep green valley wound between the mountains, with a river roaring through it. And all along the steep slopes, climbing up and up like the steps of a giant's staircase, were walls of stone.
Terraces,
said Mrs. Claus.
People built those long, long ago, so they could grow potatoes and corn on the side of a mountain.
A sleigh needs a flat place to land, and there is not much flat ground in the Andes. But one old terrace was wide and grassy, and the four reindeer came down onto it as gently as falling leaves.
Santa climbed out and took a deep breath. Then another. Then another.
The air is thin up here,
he puffed.
Even thinner than in the Himalayas.
Then we'll walk slowly,
said Mrs. Claus, buttoning her cloak.
The orchid is even higher. We'll have to climb.
Then she looked at the four reindeer, already nibbling the grass on the old terrace.
The sleigh can't go up there,
she said.
It's far too steep and rocky. But you can.
Santa unbuckled the harnesses, one by one. Dasher shook herself all over, jingle, jingle, and Comet stretched her long legs.
Reindeer are made for cold mountains,
said Mrs. Claus.
Their hooves spread out wide, like snowshoes, and grip the rocks.
Up you get, then,
said Santa, and he helped Mrs. Claus climb onto Comet's back.
In some parts of the world, people really do ride reindeer,
she said, settling in.
Far away in Siberia and Mongolia, reindeer herders ride them through the forests.
Santa tried to climb onto Dasher. He tried once, and then twice, and the third time Dasher gave a polite little sidestep, and Santa sat down in the grass with a thump.
On second thought,
he said, brushing off his coat,
I'll walk beside you, old girl.
Dasher snorted, and it sounded very much like a laugh.

So up the mountain they went: Mrs. Claus riding Comet, Santa walking beside Dasher with one hand on her harness, and Dancer and Vixen following behind, their knees going click, click, click on the rocky path.
The path wound up the mountainside, past old stone walls and twisted little trees with peeling, papery red bark, layer upon layer, like the pages of an old book.
Queñua trees,
said Mrs. Claus, touching the bark.
They grow higher up the mountains than almost any other tree in the world.
The sun was hot on their faces, but the air was cool, and every time they stopped to rest, the wind felt like it had come straight off the ice.
They came around a bend onto a steep, rocky slope covered in tall grass. And Santa stopped so suddenly that Dasher bumped her nose into his back.
Linnea,
he said.
Look.

All across the slope, rising out of the grass on tall, straight stems, were flowers. Big flowers, bigger than her hand, glowing orange like little flames. Each one had three long points, swept back like the tail feathers of a bird. And when the wind moved them, they flickered. A shimmer of purple ran across the orange, then vanished, then came back again, as if the flowers were made of fire and silk at the same time.
Oh,
said Mrs. Claus. She slid off Comet's back and sat right down in the grass.
Oh, Kris.

She took out her magnifying glass and leaned close. The orange petals were covered in thousands of tiny purple hairs, so small you could hardly see them. When the light hit them from one side, the flower glowed orange. From the other side, it shimmered purple.
It's the King of the Masdevallias,
she whispered.
Masdevallia veitchiana. People here call it gallo-gallo, the rooster flower, because it looks like a rooster's bright red comb. People have loved it for a very long time.
Well, that settles it,
said Santa happily.
We've found our orchid! Let's get the scroll out.
Mrs. Claus unrolled the scroll and held it up beside the glowing orange flowers. Then she looked at the tiny painting at the bottom: the little white flower in the green marsh, beneath the ice.
She shook her head slowly.
It isn't this one, Kris. Ours is small. And white. And it lives up there.
She pointed up the mountain, past the grass and the rocks, to where the snow and ice began.
Santa looked at the King of the Masdevallias, and then up at the cold, high slopes.
You mean,
he said,
we have to leave the most beautiful orchid we've ever seen, to go and look for a little white one?
I'm afraid so,
said Mrs. Claus, smiling. But first she drew the King in her sketchbook, as carefully as she had drawn every orchid on their journey. Then she bowed her head to the shimmering flowers.
Thank you for being so beautiful,
she said.
Even if you aren't the one we came for.

They climbed on. The trees disappeared, and then the bushes, and soon there was nothing but golden grass, stiff and spiky, rippling in the wind like the fur of a giant animal. A big bird with enormous black wings and a white collar glided past, far overhead, without ever flapping once.
A condor,
said Mrs. Claus.
One of the largest flying birds in the world.
Show-off,
puffed Santa, leaning on a rock.
From behind the rock, a furry gray face with long ears popped up and stared at him.
A rabbit!
said Santa.
A vizcacha,
laughed Mrs. Claus.
It looks like a rabbit, but it's a cousin of the chinchilla.
The vizcacha twitched its long whiskers, decided Santa was not very interesting, and hopped away.

Higher still, the land flattened out into a wide, wet valley. Little streams wound through it, bright with snowmelt, and the ground was covered in round, shiny green cushions that squished underfoot. All around the edge of the valley, alpacas were grazing: brown ones and white ones and black ones and spotted ones, with fluffy topknots and soft, curious eyes. A few tall llamas stood among them like watchful aunties.

The alpacas lifted their heads all at once and stared at the four reindeer. The reindeer stared back. For a long moment, nobody moved. Then the smallest alpaca took three careful steps forward and made a soft humming sound, mmmm, like someone humming a song with their mouth closed.
Alpacas hum when they're curious,
said Mrs. Claus.

Vixen lowered her head and hummed back, or tried to. It came out more like a snort. A tall llama strolled over and sniffed Dancer's antlers from top to bottom, very seriously, as if she had never seen anything so strange in her whole life.
And beyond the valley, so close it seemed you could touch it, rose a mountain of blue-white ice.
A little girl in a bright woven skirt and a round hat came running down the slope toward them, followed by an old woman wrapped in a striped shawl, and a man carrying a long stick.
¡Buenos días!
called the girl. Then, looking at Santa's red coat and white beard, she stopped. Her eyes went very wide.
Buenos días,
said Mrs. Claus, smiling.
That means good morning in Spanish,
she whispered to Santa.
The grandmother looked them up and down, slowly and carefully, the way people do when they have lived on a mountain all their lives. Then she smiled too.
Imaynalla,
she said.
That's how we say hello in Quechua, our first language. It means, how are you?

Her name was Mamá Rosa, and the girl was Killa, which means moon in Quechua. Killa's father, Tomás, herded the family's alpacas here every day. They invited Santa and Mrs. Claus to sit with them on a woven blanket, out of the wind, and poured them cups of hot muña tea that smelled of mint and mountains. There were boiled potatoes too, little ones, yellow and purple and red.
We have hundreds of kinds of potatoes in the Andes,
said Tomás proudly.
More than anywhere in the world.
Killa couldn't stop staring at the reindeer. When Comet stepped closer, her knees went click, click, click, and Killa gasped and clapped her hands over her mouth.
¡Escucha!
she said.
Listen! Their knees make music!
Are they cousins of the llamas?
she asked.
Not cousins,
said Mrs. Claus.

Llamas and alpacas come from the camel family, and reindeer come from the deer family. But they're a lot alike. They all live in cold, high places, they all eat what grows there, and they all help people carry things.
Tomás laughed.
Our llamas carry potatoes,
he said.
Yours carry presents.
Mrs. Claus gave them a tin of her ginger cookies. Killa ate one in three bites and then politely asked for another.
Then Mrs. Claus showed them the scroll and the tiny painting of the white flower.
Killa clapped her hands.
La florcita del bofedal!
she said.
The little flower of the marsh! I know where it lives. It hides in the cushions, near the ice. Nobody ever looks at it.
Mamá Rosa nodded. She looked out across the green marsh, where the streams sparkled, and up at the glacier.
This bofedal gives water to our alpacas and to our village, all year long,
she said.
The water comes from the ice. But the ice is smaller now than when I was a girl. Much smaller.
She was quiet for a moment.
We take good care of the bofedal. Everything here depends on it, even the little flower.

Mrs. Claus looked down at the scroll, at the sixth painting, so faded that they had almost missed it. She thought of the shrinking ice, and she wondered whether a painting could fade the way a glacier does, a little more every year. She held the old paper a little more carefully after that.
Will you show us?
asked Mrs. Claus.
Your reindeer may come too,
said Mamá Rosa.
But they must walk on the stones, not on the green cushions. The cushions grow very, very slowly. One hoof in the wrong place can break what took many years to grow.
So Mrs. Claus led the four reindeer along the stony edge of the marsh, one careful step at a time, and not one hoof touched a cushion.
Killa led them across the marsh, hopping from stone to stone as easily as a vizcacha. Santa followed more slowly, and one of his big boots went squelch into the cold water.
At the far edge of the marsh, where the green cushions met the gray stones below the ice, Killa knelt down.
Here,
she said proudly.
Santa knelt beside her and looked. Then he looked again.

Tucked into the shiny green cushions was a tiny plant, no taller than his thumb. It had a little flat circle of small, tough leaves, pressed close to the ground. And from the middle of the circle rose one short, fat spike, crowded with little flowers, pale white and greenish, like a tiny bunch of frost.
That's it?
said Santa. He tried very hard to sound polite.
That's the sixth Snow Orchid?
Most people say that,
said a voice behind them.
They turned around.

Standing on the stones at the edge of the ice was an animal like a small, slender camel, with long legs and a long neck and soft fur the color of golden sand, with a white bib on its chest. Its eyes were huge and dark and fringed with long lashes. Around its edges, the air shimmered, the way air shimmers over a stone in the sun.
A vicuña,
whispered Killa.
But I've never seen one shimmer like that.
The four reindeer, waiting on the stones at the edge of the marsh, lowered their antlers in a slow, deep bow. The vicuña dipped its long golden neck back to them.
Cousins of the snow,
it said.
You have come a very long way for your sister.
Most travelers walk right past my flower,
said the vicuña. Its voice was light and quick, as if it were trying not to laugh.
They come all this way and they stop down there, at the King, with their mouths wide open. And then they go home and say, there were no orchids up at the top, only grass and ice.
It tilted its head.
You walked past the King. Why?
Because the scroll told us to,
said Santa honestly.
Though I'll admit, I wanted to stay.
The vicuña's eyes sparkled.
An honest answer. Now. Kneel down, both of you, and look. Really look. And then tell me if you are still disappointed.
Mrs. Claus was already lying on her tummy in the wet cushions, her magnifying glass held to her eye. Santa lay down beside her, which took a while, and a good deal of puffing.
And through the glass, the little white flower changed.

Each tiny bloom was smaller than a grain of rice. But each one was perfect. Its lip curled up like a little hood, and all along its edges ran a fringe, fine as lace. And covering the inside of the lip were hairs so small they looked like strings of tiny glass beads, every one sparkling with frost.
Kris,
breathed Mrs. Claus.
It's covered in jewels.
What is she called?
asked Santa.
Scientists call her Myrosmodes,
said Mrs. Claus, still peering through her glass.
You say it my-ROSS-mo-deez. This one is Myrosmodes paludosa. Paludosa means 'of the marshes.'
She smiled.
But in my notebook, I'm going to call her the Snow Orchid of the Andes.
And we call her la florcita del bofedal,
said Killa.
The little flower of the marsh.
Every night, the marsh freezes solid,
said the vicuña.

Every morning, the sun melts it again. The wind never stops. The sunlight up here would burn your nose in an hour. Almost no flower in the world can live where she lives. Scientists have found her cousins blooming higher than almost any other orchid on Earth, right up against the ice.
Santa looked at the tiny flower for a long, long time.
And look,
said Mrs. Claus.
The flowers at the top of the spike are open, and the ones at the bottom are still closed. She blooms from the top down. Most flowers on a spike do it the other way around.
Of course she does,
said the vicuña.
She has never done anything the ordinary way.
Just then, a small fly landed on the spike and crawled across the beaded flowers.
A fly!
said Killa.
Scientists who studied one of her cousins found that bumblebees didn't visit it at all,
said Mrs. Claus.
Flies and wasps did. Up here, she takes whatever friends she can get.
She took out her sketchbook and began to draw, slowly and carefully: the flat little circle of leaves, the short spike rising from its center, the fringed lip with its strings of beads.
So,
said the vicuña softly.
Are you still disappointed?
Santa sat up, wiping the marsh water off his beard.
No,
he said.
I feel a little ashamed that I was. She's the most surprising thing I've seen on this whole journey.
That is her lesson,
said the vicuña.

The King teaches you to gasp. My flower teaches you to kneel. The most wonderful things are not always the biggest or the brightest. Sometimes you have to get down on your knees in the cold and look closer, and the world opens up like a door. And when you truly see something, you can't help being thankful for it.
Mrs. Claus looked down at her drawing. The flat circle of leaves. The spike rising from the middle. The fringe, curling like a little wave. All together, the lines made a shape.
She looked at the scroll. The sixth rune, glowing silver-blue beside the tiny painting, was the very same shape.
Gratitude,
she whispered.
Her rune means Gratitude. It means thank you.
The vicuña bent its long neck down to the little orchid and breathed on it, very gently. A single crystal of frost lifted from the beaded lip and floated up into the air, sparkling like a tiny star.
This frost will never melt,
said the vicuña.
Not as long as someone remembers to look closely at small things. Take it, and the lesson with it.
Mrs. Claus held out one last little glass bottle, and the frost crystal drifted inside. She corked it and wrote on the label: Snow Orchid of the Andes. Gratitude (thank you).

Then she opened her aurora lantern, and a single drop of northern light floated out and settled on the tiny white spike. For a moment, the smallest flower at the top of the world glowed brighter than the glacier behind it.
Thank you for teaching us,
said Mrs. Claus.
Sulpayki,
said Killa, which means thank you in Quechua. And she said it to the flower.
When they looked up, the vicuña was gone. Only a few hoofprints remained on the stones, and then not even those.
