Mrs. Claus rode Comet back along the stones, with Santa and Dasher beside them, and they said goodbye to Mamá Rosa and Tomás. The smallest alpaca hummed at Vixen one last time, and Vixen snorted back. Killa walked with them all the way down to the King of the Masdevallias, still flickering orange and purple in the late afternoon light.
I'm going to tell everyone at school about the little flower,
she said.
And I'll make sure no one steps on it.
I think,
said Mrs. Claus,
that the little flower is lucky to have you.

Back on the old terrace, Santa buckled the four reindeer into their harnesses again, and the sleigh rose into an evening sky streaked with pink and gold. Below them, Killa waved and waved until she was a tiny dot. Far above, the glacier glowed rose-pink in the last of the sun.
Mrs. Claus took out her six treasures and held them in her lap: five little glass bottles and one paper envelope. Then she counted the runes on the scroll, one by one.
Wait,
she said.
Balance. Listen. Belong. Hope.
She touched the last bottle, where the frost crystal sparkled.
And Gratitude.
Six,
said Santa thoughtfully, looking at the six little treasures.
Like the six points of a snowflake.
Mrs. Claus looked at him for a long moment, and then down at the six runes in her sketchbook. She didn't say anything at all. But she was smiling.
Far away in the north, in a quiet barn at the top of the world, Blitzen lifted her head and pricked her ears, as if someone very far away had called her name.

Summer ended at the North Pole the way it always does. Little by little, the sun sank lower in the sky, circling closer and closer to the edge of the world. Then, one evening near the end of September, it slipped below the horizon, painting the whole sky pink and gold and orange, and it didn't come back up. The long night was beginning again.
And as the sky grew dark, something wonderful returned.
One night, a single pale green ribbon appeared above the barn. Then another, and another, until the whole sky was swirling with green and violet and pink. The elves ran out into the snow, cheering.
The northern lights are back!
Tonight,
said Mrs. Claus, looking up.
It has to be tonight.

The barn was warm and golden with lantern light. The whole herd stood in their stalls, ears pricked and eyes shining, watching. The elves crowded in the doorway, their cap bells jingling softly, and Snowbell had come all the way down from the library, hugging the Saga of Winter's Bloom to her chest.
In the center of the barn stood a low wooden table, and on it Mrs. Claus set out everything they had brought home from their journey around the world.

There was a crystal bowl, so clear that it seemed to be made of ice. There were her six treasures from the journey: five little glass bottles, corked and labeled in her neat handwriting, and one paper envelope holding a silver-veined leaf. There was a little jug of fresh water from the melt ponds on the sea ice, where the summer snow had melted into puddles as blue as a robin's egg. There was a jar of golden honey from her greenhouse bees. And there was one of her aurora lanterns from the greenhouse, glowing softly with its wisp of captured northern light.
Last of all, she laid her sketchbook open beside the bowl, at the page with all six runes.
Blitzen watched every move from her stall. Her new antlers stood tall and branching above her head, smooth and pale and clean now that their velvet was gone. And still completely blank.
Mrs. Claus took a deep breath. Everyone grew quiet.
This part,
she said softly,
is the Earth's part. The part that comes from the living world.
She poured the clear melt-pond water into the crystal bowl, trickle, trickle. Then she uncorked the first little bottle, and a breath of the Fairy Slipper's sweet scent drifted down into the water.
For the Fairy Slipper,
she said,
who stores the summer's light and waits through the dark. Wait.
The water in the bowl shimmered, just a little.
She uncorked the second bottle, and the single drop of snowmelt fell in, plink.
For the Ice Orchid, who blooms at exactly the right moment, between the snow and the sun. Balance.
The third, and a wisp of waterfall mist curled down onto the water, humming faintly.
For the Frost Lantern, who reads the mountain and grows where the water sings. Listen.
The fourth: the glowing thread from the forest's web, uncoiling softly into the bowl.
For the Phantom Orchid, held up by the whole forest. Belong.
And the fifth: the old silver-veined leaf.
For the Rattlesnake Plantain, who stays green under the snow all winter long. Hope.
Last of all, she uncorked the sixth bottle, and the tiny crystal of frost from the top of the world tumbled into the bowl, glittering like a star.
For the Snow Orchid of the Andes, the smallest flower at the top of the world, who taught us to kneel down, look closer, and be thankful. Gratitude.
With each one, the water glowed a little brighter, first pale gold, then warmer, until the whole bowl shone like a cup of sunrise.

Then Mrs. Claus dipped a spoon into the honey and stirred it in, slowly, a golden ribbon curling through the light. And finally, she opened the little door of the aurora lantern, and one tiny wisp of green northern light floated out and drifted down, down, down into the bowl.
The light in the bowl turned from gold to rose.
Now,
said Mrs. Claus, and she looked at Santa with shining eyes.
Now it needs the Sky's part, Kris. Your part.
Santa stepped forward. He didn't say a magic word. He simply held his big hands out over the bowl, and he closed his eyes and smiled.
And from far away, something began to arrive.

It came in through the cracks of the barn roof, and the gaps around the door, and the high window: tiny sparks of light, like fireflies, hundreds and then thousands of them, floating in from every direction, from every corner of the world. They swirled gently around Santa's hands and drifted down into the bowl, one by one, tink, tink, tink.
What are they?
whispered Snowbell.
Kindness,
said Santa softly.

That's where Christmas magic comes from, you know. Every time a child somewhere shares a toy, or helps a friend who has fallen down, or comforts someone who is sad, or feeds the birds in winter, or waters a little plant, or says sorry, or makes someone feel welcome, a tiny spark of light flies all the way to the North Pole. I keep them all. That's what I mean when I say a child has been nice.
He opened his eyes and looked at all the elves and the reindeer.
Being nice doesn't mean being perfect,
he said.
Nobody is perfect, not even Santa. Every child is still learning. Being nice means being a kind part of the world, a good thread in the web.
The last sparks drifted into the bowl. The light inside glowed so brightly now that the whole barn turned rosy pink, and every face in it was smiling.
The Earth's part,
said Mrs. Claus.
And the Sky's part.
Together,
said Santa.

Then Mrs. Claus reached into her apron pocket, the very same pocket she had reached into on the night Blitzen first couldn't fly, and took out a soft little bundle of reindeer lichen, pale gray-green and crinkly, like a tiny forest of coral. And she set it gently into the glowing bowl.
For a moment, nothing happened.
Then the lichen began to glow: gold, then rose, then the pale green of the northern lights. Tiny patterns flickered across its little branches, like leaf veins and frost and fine white threads.
And then it began to grow.

It grew slowly at first, a little curl here, a little branch there. Then faster, and faster, crinkly gray-green branches spreading and sprouting and tumbling, filling the bowl and spilling over the edge, crinkle, crinkle, crinkle, across the table and down onto the straw.
Oh my!
cried Snowbell, jumping back.

The elves gasped. And then they laughed and cheered, because the lichen kept on growing, a soft, glowing, sweet-smelling carpet spreading across the barn floor, smelling of snow and forests and summer meadows and starlight.
In real life,
said Mrs. Claus, laughing with delight,
lichen grows only a tiny bit each year. This part is magic!
Baskets!
called Santa.
Quick, everybody, baskets!

The elves ran for their baskets and began to harvest the glowing lichen, filling basket after basket, giggling as it kept growing around their ankles. And they carried it to every single stall: to Dasher and Dancer, to Prancer and Vixen, to Comet and Cupid and Donner, to old Evenstar, to Whistler, Bramble and Starbloom, to little Lilt, and last of all, to Blitzen.
All of them?
asked Snowbell.
All of them,
said Mrs. Claus.
Blitzen felt the world's wobble first, because she's the most sensitive. But every reindeer felt it a little. This is for all of them.

The reindeer bent their heads and began to eat. Crunch, crunch, crunch. All along the row of stalls, every reindeer in the herd munched happily on glowing lichen, and with every bite, their eyes grew brighter, and their coats began to shine.
Mrs. Claus knelt beside Blitzen, holding a handful of the glowing lichen in her palm.
If you're willing,
she whispered.
Blitzen looked at her for a long moment with her deep, shining eyes. Then she leaned forward and took a bite. Crunch, crunch.
And the light flowed straight through her, from her nose to the tip of her tail, as if she had swallowed a little piece of the northern lights.

She shivered once. She lifted her head. And then, slowly, she stepped out of her stall, across the glowing lichen, past the elves, through the wide barn doors, and out into the snow, under the dancing northern lights.
Everyone followed her outside, holding their breath.
Blitzen stood alone in the snow and lifted her face to the sky. The green and violet and pink light poured down over her, over her shining coat and her tall new antlers.
And on her antlers, something began to appear.

Thin silver lines, glowing softly in the aurora light. One rune, near the base of her right antler: a little slipper-shaped cup under a sweeping crown. Wait. Then another, a little higher: a star of five petals around a round cup. Balance. Then a little hood with a curling ear and a lip spreading below. Listen. Then a single stem with flowers held all along it. Belong. Then a straight stem with a spiral winding up it. Hope. And at the very tip, a little circle of leaves with a fringed spike rising from it. Gratitude. They were the six Snow Orchids themselves, blooming in silver light.

And then, at the very top of her tallest branches, three more runes appeared, glowing brighter than all the rest. A single straight line. An upside-down antler. And a point, rising like the top of a mountain.
Winter. Root. Flight,
whispered Snowbell.
Just like Firstlight's.
Mrs. Claus stepped close, her sketchbook pressed to her heart, her eyes full of tears, and she read the whole message, the one Firstlight had been waiting a thousand years to tell them:
Wait. Balance. Listen. Belong. Hope. Gratitude. Through winter, from the root, comes flight.
She turned to Santa.
That's the secret, Kris,
she said.

Flight isn't only magic from the sky. It grows from roots, from the living Earth and everything in it, all connected. A reindeer flies when the Earth and the Sky meet inside her. Blitzen lost her connection to the Earth. And no single orchid could give it back. It took all six lessons together.
Tiny Tamsin tugged at the hem of Mrs. Claus's cloak.
But what does it mean?
she asked.
Mrs. Claus knelt down in the snow beside her and counted on her fingers, one finger for each orchid.
Wait,
she said,
like the Fairy Slipper, who holds summer's light all winter long and blooms at just the right moment. Good things take time.
Balance, like the Ice Orchid, who blooms in the short time between the frost and the summer heat. Not too much, and not too little.
Listen, like the Frost Lantern, who grows only where the snowmelt trickles. If you pay attention to the world around you, it will show you the way.
Belong, like the Phantom Orchid, held by her fungus and her forest. Nobody grows all alone. We all need each other.
Hope, like the Rattlesnake Plantain, whose leaves stay green under the snow all winter. Even in the longest, darkest winter, spring is coming.
Then she held up one finger on her other hand.

And Gratitude, which means thank you, like the little Snow Orchid of the Andes. She lives in the coldest, windiest place you can imagine, and she's beautiful anyway, if you kneel down and look closer. When you really look at the world, you find so much to be thankful for.
She folded her two hands together, all six fingers tucked inside.

And when you put them all together, you get the whole secret: through winter, from the root, comes flight. When we wait, keep our balance, listen, remember that we belong to each other, never stop hoping, and remember to say thank you, even the longest winter ends, and we can fly again.
Tiny Tamsin thought about that for a long moment.
So Blitzen needed the whole wide world to help her fly,
she said.
Exactly,
said Mrs. Claus, and she kissed the top of Tamsin's curly head.
Santa wiped his eyes with the back of his mitten.
And all of us together,
he said.

Blitzen lowered her head. Her hooves began to tingle, tickle-tickle-tickle, like snowflakes landing on her toes. The tingle rose up through her legs and along her back, all the way to the tips of her shining antlers. And then, softly at first, her hooves began to click. Click. Click-click. Click-click-click, faster and faster, like a drumroll, until they were clicking in the very same rhythm as the hooves of every reindeer around her.
She took a deep breath that puffed out in a long white cloud. She bent her knees.
And she leaped.
This time, she didn't come down.

Up she rose, past the barn roof, up into the swirling green and violet light, her antlers glowing with silver runes, turning a great, happy circle in the sky high above the North Pole. Her bells rang out, clear and bright, jingle-jingle-jingle, across the whole village.
And then something happened that nobody, not even Snowbell, had ever seen before.

The runes on Blitzen's antlers grew brighter and brighter, until they lifted away into the sky like sparks from a fire. They spun and drifted and found their places, one after another: Wait at the center, then Balance, then Listen, then Belong, then Hope, and Gratitude at the very tip, all lined up along a single shining arm. And then the arm was mirrored, and then there were two arms, and then three, and four, and five, and six.

High above the North Pole, in the middle of the northern lights, hung an enormous snowflake made of silver light. Every one of its six arms carried all six runes, from Wait near its heart to Gratitude at its tips. And at the very center, where all six arms met, there was no rune at all. Only a soft, warm light, glowing brighter than all the rest.
The Snowflake of Six,
whispered Snowbell, her spectacles shining.
It's in the oldest books in the library. I've seen it a hundred times, and I never knew what it meant.
Every snowflake in the world has six arms,
said Mrs. Claus softly.
Never five. That's why the old message couldn't be finished without her. Five runes could never make a snowflake.
What's in the middle?
asked Tiny Tamsin, pointing at the warm light at the snowflake's heart.
Joy,
said Mrs. Claus.
Joy isn't a rune all by itself. It's what you feel when everything comes together: when we wait, keep our balance, listen, belong to each other, keep hoping, and say thank you. All six at once.
Santa looked up at the great silver snowflake.
And no two snowflakes in the whole world are alike,
he said,

but every single one has six arms. Six places, all different: Lapland, the Himalayas, Japan, Mount Rainier, the Rocky Mountains and the Andes. And all the people and creatures who helped us along the way. Every one of them different. And it took every one of them to make one snowflake.

Blitzen flew straight through the middle of the great silver snowflake, and it burst into a thousand tiny glittering flakes that drifted down over the whole village, landing on the rooftops and the elves' caps and Santa's beard, each one sparkling for a moment before it melted away.

The elves cheered so loudly that snow slid off the rooftops, whumph! Snowbell's spectacles fogged up completely. Mrs. Claus laughed and cried at the same time, and Santa threw his head back and laughed his deep, round, rumbly laugh,
Ho, ho, ho!
for the first time in a very, very long time.

One by one, the other reindeer leaped up to join her: Dasher and Dancer, Prancer and Vixen, Comet and Cupid and Donner, then Evenstar, Whistler, Bramble and Starbloom, and last of all, little Lilt, flying for the very first time in her life, wobbling a bit and then soaring. And now, in the aurora light, everyone could see that all of their antlers were glowing with silver runes too.
Kris,
said Mrs. Claus,
let's fly with them.

So the elves brought out the sleigh, and for the first time in a long time, all eight reindeer stood together in their harnesses, with Blitzen at the very front. Santa and Mrs. Claus climbed in and tucked the wool blanket over their knees. Santa raised the silver harness bells, and they answered, clear and bright. Then he gave the reins a gentle shake, not to command, but to invite.
The reindeer leaned forward as one. And together, they leaped onto the auroral road and rose up into the shining sky.

Down in the snow, the elves stood watching the sleigh's bright trail climb into the lights. Bob Mookie began to sing in his big, warm voice, and Hazel Crumb joined in beside him, their two voices rising up after the sleigh while everyone else stood still to listen.

High above the North Pole, the sleigh glided along the auroral road. Mrs. Claus looked down over the side, and in the shimmering light, she could almost see them, far away, all around the world, the six orchids getting ready for their seasons.
In a Lapland spruce forest, the Fairy Slipper was unfolding one brand-new leaf in the cool autumn moss, ready to stay green beneath the snow.
On a Himalayan mountainside, the Ice Orchid's little cone-shaped bulbs were resting, waiting for the snow to come and go again.
On a wet cliff in Japan, the Frost Lantern was going quietly to sleep as the first frosts touched the waterfall.
On the slopes of Mount Rainier, beneath the fallen leaves, the Phantom Orchid's hidden threads stretched from tree to tree, holding hands with the whole forest.
And in a valley of the Rocky Mountains, beneath an old cedar, a colony of Rattlesnake Plantain was keeping its silver-veined leaves green as the first snowflakes began to fall.

And far to the south, in a frozen marsh below a glacier in the Andes, where spring was only beginning, a tiny white flower sat tucked among the green cushions, glittering with frost, in a place where hardly anyone would ever think to look.
All different. All far apart. And all part of the same great web.

Mrs. Claus smiled to herself. She knew they were there, every one of them, safe in their own wild places. And she knew something else too. These six were only the beginning. All around the world, wherever the snow melts in spring, there are many, many more orchids: on mountain ledges and in mossy forests, beside cold streams and in wet meadows, more than anyone has ever counted. And every one of them, she was sure, holds a lesson of its own.
Someday,
she whispered,
I'd like to go and learn from all of them.
Then we'll have to make sure they're still there when you do,
said Santa.

And Mrs. Claus knew he was right. That might be the most important lesson of all. Every orchid needs its forest and its fungus, its pollinator and its snow. And it needs people who care about the wild places where it grows. If those places are kept safe, the lessons will be waiting, one for every spring, for as long as the snow keeps melting.

When the sleigh landed back at the barn, there was still a great heap of glowing lichen left over, far more than the reindeer could ever eat. So the next morning, the elves packed it into soft bundles and flew it far to the south, to the rocky tundra, where real lichen grows. There they tucked it carefully among the stones, a little here and a little there, so that the land could have some of the magic back.
Take only what you need,
Mrs. Claus told them,
and give back the rest.
A few days later, Snowbell came knocking at the cottage door, her frost-crystal spectacles fogging up in the warm kitchen.
Linnea,
she said shyly,
may I ask you something? Your field notebook. Would you let me keep it in the Library of Lost Winters?
Mrs. Claus looked down at her sketchbook. Its pages were soft and crinkled from rain and waterfall spray and snow.
My messy old notebook?
It isn't messy. It's precious,
said Snowbell.

It tells where each orchid grows, and when it blooms, and who visits it, and what it needs. The old reindeer keepers wrote their lessons down so they would never be forgotten. Someday, somebody will want to find a Snow Orchid, or help one. Your notebook will show them the way.

So that very afternoon, Linnea's field notebook took its place on a shelf in the Library of Lost Winters, right beside the old blue book, where anyone who wanted to learn about the Snow Orchids could find it.

The weeks went by. The long polar night settled over the North Pole, and the northern lights danced every night. In the workshop, the elves hammered and painted and wrapped. In the post office, the letters piled up in their cubbies. And in the barn, eight reindeer practiced flying every single evening, their antlers glowing with silver runes.
At last, it was Christmas Eve.

The sleigh was piled so high with presents for every child in the world that it took all eight reindeer to pull it. And at the very front of the team, her new antlers shining with runes, stood Blitzen.
Mrs. Claus came out to say goodbye, her cranberry cloak swishing and her silver twinflower brooch glinting in the aurora light. She kissed Blitzen on the nose, and then Santa on the cheek.
Fly safely, Kris,
she said.
Always,
said Santa.

He gave the reins a gentle shake. The reindeer leaned forward as one, and with a jingle of bells, they leaped onto the auroral road and rose into the glowing sky, past the rooftops and the chimneys and the arched window of the Library of Lost Winters, where Snowbell was waving with both hands.
Up and up they flew, and away over the sleeping world.

As they crossed the first sleeping town, its rooftops white with snow, Santa leaned over the side of the sleigh. His voice was soft, so soft that only the night really heard it. But somehow, it carried all the way to every child, everywhere.
May your hearts be light,
he said,
your days be kind, and may wonder find you wherever you are.

Blitzen's hooves struck the auroral road, strong and sure. The team surged forward. And across the quiet world, where snow waited for the dawn, where children dreamed and forests kept their secrets and orchids rested beneath winter's blanket, the old magic rose once more. It wasn't new at all. Only remembered.
The flight went on.
